MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. I mean among the things that were made public by a Trump donor were text messages in which she asked him to give her $100,000 to pay off credit card debt and asked not to put some of these things in writing because it could endanger her job.
Are you comfortable with any U.S. official asking someone to pay off debt in exchange for access to government officials?

SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: No, I'm not. And, you know, we're going to be back after the elections. But for the next three weeks, we're going to be out campaigning across the country. And I'm sure we'll discuss that later.

But the focus today is making sure that the American people know just how far to the left the Democrats have gone. And they are now the party, and they have – they have a manifesto, and you highlighted one of the candidates from Florida, the Democrat nominee in Florida.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: They want to eliminate Immigrations and Customs Enforcement, open the border. They want to open the prisons, put these people into our communities. They want to defund the military, defund the police, raise taxes to pay for health care for illegal immigrants and have boys in girl's locker rooms.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well –
SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: And when you were on with Murphy, and you asked about the military –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: The Democrats have blocked the National Defense Authorization Act.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: He says, well, we ought to not fund things.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well –
SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: This is the first time in 65 years that we've not passed a National Defense Authorization Act, which funds the military and makes sure they have what they need –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: To be able to be the war fighters that they are.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: And yet the Democrats are all voting no on supporting our troops.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, he said that he did want more information. He said that briefings weren't being shared, details weren't being shared. So, approving money without those briefings is something he said he was not willing to do. Would you ask the administration to be more forthcoming and give details, including on these damage to bases?
SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: Well, you're talking appropriations. I'm talking about the actual authorization act to get – make sure the military has what they want.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Got it.

SENATOR JOHN BARRASSO: The Democrats in the Senate are so afraid of these candidates who have won nominations and primary elections that when those candidates and their manifesto calls for defunding the military, all of the Democrats in the Senate voted against the National Defense Authorization Act. And that's just wrong.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, Senator Barrasso, we will watch what you get done in – on the campaign trail and when we get back to work in November. Thank you for your time.
We'll be right back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: We turn now to Congressman Chris Pappas, who's running for the U.S. Senate in his native New Hampshire. He joins us this morning from Manchester.
Good morning.
REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS (D-NH): Hi, Margaret. Good morning.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, CBS projects that New Hampshire is no longer a toss-up but lean Democrat. So, what are you focused on in these final weeks of the campaign?

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: Well, we're taking nothing for granted in this race because New Hampshire's a purple state. And we're an all election day state where we don't have early voting generally in New Hampshire. So, it's focused on how we get to those independent swing voters, how we energize the base, how we reach out to Republicans of the next 23 days, to win a tough race.
Our Senate race in 2016 in New Hampshire was decided by 1,017 votes. I'm up against a candidate with a very famous political pedigree in New Hampshire. He's been a U.S. senator before.

But this isn't about going back to the failed politicians with failed ideas from the past. It's about looking ahead to the future. How we muster the courage to stand up to a reckless administration that's making life more expensive, how we fight to lower costs.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: How we connect with everyday granite staters about the kind of future we can build together.

So, I'm hopeful about where we're going to end up at the end of this thing, but we've got to put in the work over the next 23 days in order to change things in Washington and deliver the results New Hampshire deserves.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, Democrats do seem nationally to be running on an anti-Trump agenda in your particular race. You mentioned John Sununu, you're opponent. He doesn't make that strategy easy because he used to be a never Trumper, he criticizes the trade war with Canada, he doesn't like Trump sending $5,000 checks out. He said it was a mistake to start the war with Iran without a strategy for the Strait of Hormuz. I mean he has distanced himself in some ways for the president, though he is endorsed by Mr. Trump.
How do you split that in the minds of the Republicans that you are trying to win over?

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: John Sununu has said it out loud. He said that this race is important to Donald Trump's agenda, and to protect the gains that Donald Trump has made for the American people. You know, I don't know what those gains are, because if you were paying $1,000 to fill up your home heating oil tank, or $6.50 to put diesel in your car for every gallon, or housing costs that are through the roof, you're not feeling like you're winning right now.
So, the fact is, Donald Trump has said this, that pretend I'm on the ballot.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: He's on the ballot through candidates like John Sununu, who will maintain his majority in the U.S. Senate, will make it harder for us to hold this administration to account, to address the culture of corruption in Washington and fight to lower costs for New Hampshire families.

So, John Sununu stands with Trump in this campaign. He's been supporting his agenda. The fact is, the last time he was in office, he stood with George W. Bush for forever wars, privatizing Social Security and tax cuts for the rich. That didn't work for New Hampshire then and he doesn't represent the kind of future we need to lower costs and get this economy working for everyone.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But if Democrats flip control of Congress, what specifically does the party want to do to stop Mr. Trump, as you just laid out? I mean is that impeachment? Is that investigation?

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: Certainly there has to be accountability. And the American people deserve to know what's going on in the government. And any sort of corruption has to be rooted out. But we have to focus like a laser on the economic challenges that people are living right now. We have to put some wins on the board for workers and the middle class.
MARGARET BRENNAN: How do you do that?

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: We can do that by building on the success of the housing bill that we passed to invest in the affordable housing stock that we need, to work to end this war and lower energy prices, to restore the cuts to health care that are kicking thousands of granite staters off of their health insurance, and making it harder for people to access the care that they need.

So, we do have to focus with everything we've got on the affordability agenda that starts in January. And I think that's both a short, medium, and long term strategy to take on the way this economy has been rigged and deliver results for middle class families and workers.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You said restore cuts to health care. I think you mean in – the enhanced premium subsidies. So you want more government spending on healthcare? Is that your platform?

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: I want New Hampshire families to be able to get a health care premium that makes sense for them, that will allow them to provide for their families. Seventeen thousand folks in my state have dropped their insurance because of the failure to extend the ACA premium subsidies.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: And we're looking at a huge cut with respect to Medicaid that's going to devastate our hospitals, health centers and nursing homes, cynically timed to kick in just after this election.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well –

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: So, it's a focus both on making the Affordable Care Act work, taking the insurance companies and pharmaceutical companies to account to lower prices, and making sure we're backstopping these cuts to Medicaid so that rural health care, health care for people in underserved areas doesn't get disrupted and, you know, destroyed by these MAGA cuts that were a part of the big, beautiful bill last year.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, if Democrats do take control, there's also going to be that question of what is the unified vision for the party, and can you unify your party? There's been a lot of focus on ICE, Immigration, and Customs Enforcement. You sponsored a bill that would redirect $75 billion in ICE funding to local law enforcement agencies. You say ICE needs reform. That's different from some of your Democratic colleagues who are saying, disband ICE entirely, including just right next door in Maine, where Troy Jackson, who's running for Senate, says you've got to break it up. Why is he wrong? Why is your approach the way to go?

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: Well, we have to be realistic. Donald Trump's going to be president for the next two years. We've got to find every point of leverage we possibly can to reign in the disgusting abuses we have seen from ICE. From next door in Biddeford, Maine, to Minneapolis, to Texas, this is unacceptable to people in New Hampshire, and it's unacceptable to voters across the political spectrum.

So, we need accountability. We need to take back the extra money that they were given in that slush fund last year. $75 billion with no stringing attached by Congress, with no meaningful oversight. We need to make sure that ICE officers are conducting themselves like our trusted local law enforcement does, making sure that they're identified, that they're – have deescalation training, that they have body cameras. All of that would be a step in the right direction.
But the fact is, this is a nation of immigrants. And we have to make sure that we are going after the worst of the worst.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: Criminals that are violating the law. While also respecting due process rights and making sure that immigrants are a part of our extended American family.
MARGARET BRENNAN: OK.

REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: And people in New Hampshire support that. And I hope we can get to the point where we're talking about immigration reform that will allow immigrants to follow a path to work hard, to earn their citizenship –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right.
REPRESENTATIVE CHRIS PAPPAS: And to ensure that our businesses can benefit from that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: Right. And then you'd have to work with a Republican president on those things.
Thank you very much for your time.
We'll be back in a moment.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

MARGARET BRENNAN: For another perspective on artificial intelligence, we spoke Friday with Shyam Sankar, the chief technology officer for the software company Palantir. We spoke about how the rapidly advancing technology should be regulated.
(BEGIN VT)

MARGARET BRENNAN: Fifty percent of those polled by CBS say A.I. will create more problems than it solves, 29 percent say it will solve more than it creates, and 21 percent just really don't know. Like, 45 percent of Americans want the government to restrict use and development of A.I.
Is your position there should not be any guardrails at this moment?
SHYAM SANKAR (CEO, Palantir Technologies Inc.): No, not at all. That's not my position.

I think the burden is absolutely on the technology industry to show the American people that there are real benefits to A.I. and not kind of ephemeral sort of benefits, like it can help me schedule travel, but actually meaningful benefits that result in job growth and prosperity for the American people. I think one of the things that's really complicated in the current discussion is that there's an unseen force driving the narrative around A.I. safety. And it's really this millenarian, doomsday cult meets messiana (ph) complex called effective altruism.

MARGARET BRENNAN: The other part of this argument would be the people who don't want guardrails are simply in it for commercial reasons. They want to keep selling chips or they just want access to market. So, that would be the counterargument to the idea that, you know, what you're saying, which is an ideological opposition to guardrails.
SHYAM SANKAR: You know, make we could just back up. And who's on the side of no guardrails?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, when – I want to get into the specifics here because even just defining what guardrails is seems really complicated and there's not even common agreement on that right now. But Jay Clayton, who is the new DNI and the new A.I. czar, said this week the focus is on control and monitoring of technologies with the potential to do harm. So, what does that look like to you? Because it sounds like he's not even sure yet.

SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I think there's a very clear view that we should be regulating the application of the technology. So, if you're going to use this in medicines, you know, the FDA, we – as a republic, we have 250 years of rich laws and history on how to manage liability. I don't want to trivialize the metaphor, but, you know, if I buy a car and the car is defective, that's the car-maker's problem. If I then use that car to go drive into my neighbor's house, that's my problem and, you know, this sort the obfuscation that the narrative is, this technology is a total difference of kind. I don't think so. I think it's a difference of degree. It –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Well, in that, humans aren't in control of it. It would be a different kind.

SHYAM SANKAR: It – no, humans are in control of it. Even if we look at the kind of salacious reporting around Hugging Face, the models did not do anything they were not instructed to do. You know, they were – the real – first, you have human error. They were not in the sandbox. They had access to the internet. It was a horrible cybersecurity configuration. Then from that perspective, they were asked to succeed a specific benchmark, and they were not given constraints on how to do that. And they said, oh, the best way to succeed at the benchmark is to get the answers to the test, and to do so.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, for that, who should take action to –
SHYAM SANKAR: I think it's a defective product. Like, if you were going to sell that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But is it up to the Justice Department to then bring suit like on the programmers? Like, who's liable for the technology not, you know, staying within the sand box?
SHYAM SANKAR: The A.I. companies, of course. In that – in that specific case it would be the A.I. companies. If another company had licensed that technology to use in another –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes.
SHYAM SANKAR: In an application, and the product worked as expected but you misused the product, then it would be you that are responsible for that.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, you believe that the existing laws on the books should be able to handle technology as it develops?

SHYAM SANKAR: I think it is a massive running head start. I think the laws on the books speak to a lot of the current considerations. Might we need a few more things on the margin? Sure. But I think we'll figure that out as we go through it.

MARGARET BRENNAN: So, let's talk about some of those things, because you were with the president when he summoned some of these A.I. leaders recently. And he asked them all to sign a pledge to "implement robust internal controls, partner with an external auditor and establish a committee to evaluate reports from auditors." That was Google, Anthropic, OpenAI, Nvidia, Elon Musk. They all signed it. Palantir, your company, didn't. Why?
SHYAM SANKAR: Those accords were for companies that actually make A.I. models, which we do not. so –
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you help to use them and build out platforms. Like, you don't see a reason for constraints there?

SHYAM SANKAR: We do have those constraints. In fact, part of that's our entire business is, how do you safely deploy these models in specific use cases. We're just not a part – we weren't asked to be a part of the accord.
MARGARET BRENNAN: But you were there at that meeting.
SHYAM SANKAR: I was.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, what happened? Like, what was the conversation?

SHYAM SANKAR: Well, the conversation was really an assertion that the American people expect A.I. to generate economic prosperity and to do so securely and that we, as companies, have an affirmative obligation to deliver on exactly those things. And that we have existing laws to look at this and that we should be all taking this quite seriously. It was a very productive conversation.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because it sounded like the White House was saying something more should be done. And now you have this new A.I. czar, Jay Clayton, going out to Silicon Valley this week. He said he's launched this 20-day review of A.I. policy. What do you hope comes of that? Or is this another one of these like blue ribbon commissions that doesn't produce anything?

SHYAM SANKAR: No, I think a lot will come up to it, which is really focused on energy and using the existing agencies and regulatory apparatus to make sure we're on top of this stuff and providing support where it's needed.

I think one of the challenges, going back to my comments in effective altruism is today the so-called independent research organizations that are overseeing this are not really independent. They have conflicts with the labs. They are made up of people with a singular world view around affective altruism, looking for the doomsday scenarios. You know, you have evaluates who are essentially pointing a loaded gun at a target saying, I can't believe the gun worked, when they should really be saying, what guardrails do we have in place? Are – you know, are these products working to the specification we've designed and what are the opportunities for misuse?
MARGARET BRENNAN: Don't you think within the current institutions there could be some sort of entity that oversees technology?

SHYAM SANKAR: I think there's going to need to be an incident response and reporting regime that creates more visibility and transparency into what you're learning in the testing well ahead of product launches, that give visibility and transparency to the government of how people are doing at implementing exactly the existing laws.
MARGARET BRENNAN: You have said recently that "the war in Iran is the first major conflict where A.I. played a central role, particularly for targeting." Do you see risks for that?

SHYAM SANKAR: Targeting is this – is kind of this very salacious word. Really, targeting is a process. And if you think about military operations, the ability to execute a thousand strikes in a single day would have taken two weeks of planning by 50 people before. And being able to do that with one person in four hours provides you a significant battlefield advantage against your adversaries.

And so it's really not about, you know, people jump immediately to something like A.I. picking the targets. That's not what's happening. It's really, given a set of effects that you want to create, I want to be able to take out the enemy's air defenses. OK, what targets relate to that? OK. How do I then push them through a process where I understand, are any of these targets on the no strike list? Are any of these targets to close to civilian infrastructure?

MARGARET BRENNAN: Yes. Well, that goes to a broader argument about the elimination of some of the people who were involved in mitigating civilian impact from strikes. That was a Pentagon decision by Secretary Hegseth. And there were so many successful strikes in terms of the targeting in Iran, but there was also, as you know, this horrific one in Minab (ph) that killed at least 123 school children. "Bloomberg" reported some personnel relied too much on the A.I. in the Maven system made by Palantir using A.I.-enabled software. Have you determined what happened there?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, we should wait for the final report. But what I can say is, that reporting's inaccurate.
MARGARET BRENNAN: The reporting from "Bloomberg" you're saying is inaccurate?

SHYAM SANKAR: Yes, it's inaccurate. And actually, the likely cause is human error. And then – and quickly following that, we actually built additional A.I. agents that did more checking. That's part of the process we don't own.
But responding to the urgency of the moment, we built additional A.I. that actually double checks more of the work outside the process that we own to ensure things like that couldn't happen again.
MARGARET BRENNAN: So, you're suggesting it was outdated intelligence or human error that fed information into the computer system? Is that what you're saying?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, we should wait for the final report, but I think we will find –
MARGARET BRENNAN: Do you know when that will be released?
SHYAM SANKAR: I don't.

MARGARET BRENNAN: Because the initial reports have been widely reported on, including on by this network. Do you see harm in that being made public soon, or is it helpful to what you say are improvements you want to make?
SHYAM SANKAR: Well, I will defer to the department on the – on the timing of that. I have no control over that. But, yes, I would love the truth to get out there.
(END VT)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Our full conversation is on our website and our YouTube channel.
We'll be right back.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)
MARGARET BRENNAN: Our Norah O'Donnell spoke to Secret Service Director Sean Curran for tonight's "60 MINUTES."
Here's a preview.
(BEGIN VC)
NORAH O'DONNELL: How would you describe the current threat environment in this country?

SEAN CURRAN, DIRECTOR, U.S. SECRET SERVICE: It's like we've never seen before. The threats on our full-time protectees are up just over 40 percent since they – than they were last year. That's a massive increase.
O'DONNELL: Sean Curran is the 28th director of the United States Secret Service. He told us, since January, there have been 10,000 threats on the people they protect.
(END VC)
MARGARET BRENNAN: "60 MINUTES" airs tonight on CBS and Paramount Plus at 7:00 p.m. Eastern.
As for us, we'll see you next week. For "FACE THE NATION," I'm Margaret Brennan.
(ANNOUNCEMENTS)

title: DHS secretary defends livestream of Fort Hood shooter's execution
summary: Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin defended the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of an ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood.
story: Washington — Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin on Sunday defended the Pentagon's plan to livestream the execution of an ex-Army major who was convicted of the 2009 killing of 13 people at Fort Hood, while saying that he doesn't see an "elevated risk" to U.S. security amid criticism.
"I think people need to understand, if you attack America, we will come after you and we will make sure that the punishment fits the crime," Mullin said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth said last week that the Pentagon planned to publicly livestream the execution of Nidal Hasan, who is set to die by firing squad on Dec. 3 in what will be the first military execution since 1961. The announcement sparked intense criticism, including from some Republicans, like Sen. Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, who urged the Pentagon to reverse the "gruesome decision," saying there is "no need to livestream any execution, including this one."

"I would expect this from terrorists and dictators, but not here in America," Murkowski wrote in a post on X. "It would give this individual, who deserves no further notoriety, the martyrdom he seeks."
While Mullin defended the Pentagon's move, he said, "No one has to watch it if they don't choose to."

"I follow President Trump. He's the commander in chief of the country, and he does a phenomenal job," Mullin said. "He leads this country with a very, very, very direct, forward, straight hand, and he's restoring America values."
Mullin added that he has "no sympathy" for Hasan, adding, "I give absolutely zero thought to the way that this man dies."
"My job as secretary of homeland security is to protect the homeland, and that's what we do," Mullin said.

The comments come as Vice President JD Vance on Friday cast some doubt on whether the Pentagon will go ahead with the plan, saying he would not tune in if the livestream happens. The vice president said Hasan committed "the worst terrorist attack on American soil outside of 9/11" when he killed 13 people and wounded more than 30 others in the attack on the Fort Hood Army base in Texas in 2009.

"So whatever the controversy is about the method of the execution, I hope that people don't forget that this is a guy who brutally murdered a lot of innocent people," Vance said. "Now that said, I mean, look, if it's ultimately livestreamed, I'm not going to be watching it."
Mr. Trump told reporters on Saturday that there are two schools of thought on whether to livestream the execution, saying, "I'll make a decision, ultimately."

title: Democrat Chris Pappas says "we're taking nothing for granted" in N.H. race
summary: Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who's running to represent New Hampshire in the Senate, said that "we're taking nothing for granted" as Election Day approaches, amid a "tough race" in the Granite State.
story: Washington — Democratic Rep. Chris Pappas, who's running to represent New Hampshire in the Senate, said on Sunday that "we're taking nothing for granted" as Election Day approaches, amid a "tough race" in the Granite State.
"I'm hopeful about where we're going to end up at the end of this thing, but we've got to put in the work over the next 23 days," Pappas said on "Face the Nation with Margaret Brennan."

Pappas, who's represented New Hampshire in the House since 2019, is facing off against former GOP Sen. John Sununu in a race that could be key to determining which party controls the Senate. And although Republicans have been eyeing a possible opportunity to flip the seat, after Democratic Sen. Jeanne Shaheen announced she wouldn't seek reelection, CBS News rates New Hampshire as leaning Democrat.

But Pappas said given New Hampshire's status as a purple state generally and the state's lack of early voting options, his campaign is taking nothing for granted. The focus now is on "how we get to those independent, swing voters, how we energize the base, how we reach out to Republicans over the next 23 days to win a tough race," he said.
Pappas noted that the 2016 Senate race in New Hampshire came down to just over 1,000 votes, and acknowledged how his opponent's family has been dominant in Granite State politics.

"I'm up against a candidate with a very famous political pedigree in New Hampshire. He's been a U.S. senator before," Pappas said. "But this isn't about going back to the failed politicians with failed ideas from the past, it's about looking ahead to the future."

Sununu, the son of former Gov. John H. Sununu and brother of former Gov. Chris Sununu, represented New Hampshire in the House and Senate until he lost his reelection bid to Shaheen in 2008. And with a record of breaking with President Trump, he's distanced himself from the president as he campaigns to return to the upper chamber amid an unpopular war with Iran and high gas prices.
But Pappas tied Sununu's campaign to the president's agenda more broadly, and positioned the contest as a larger fight for the Senate majority.

"The fact is, Donald Trump has said this, that 'pretend I'm on the ballot,'" Pappas said. "He's on the ballot through candidates like John Sununu, who will maintain his majority in the U.S. Senate, will make it harder for us to hold this administration to account to address the culture of corruption in Washington and fight to lower costs for New Hampshire families."
Asked about Democrats' priorities should they win control of the House and Senate, Pappas said "we have to focus like a laser on the economic challenges that people are living right now."

"We have to put some wins on the board for workers and the middle class," he said. "We can do that by building on the success of the housing bill that we passed to invest in the affordable housing stock that we need, to work to end this war and lower energy prices, to restore the cuts to healthcare that are kicking thousands of Granite Staters off of their health insurance and making it harder for people to access the care that they need."
On immigration enforcement, Pappas has emphasized the need for reforms, while other Democrats have called for Immigration and Customs Enforcement to be disbanded entirely.

"We have to be realistic — Donald Trump's going to be president for the next two years. We got to find every point of leverage we possibly can to rein in the disgusting abuses we have seen from ICE," Pappas said. "We have to make sure that we are going after the worst of the worst criminals that are violating the law, while also respecting due process rights and making sure that immigrants are part of our extended American family. And people in New Hampshire support that."

title: Steve Bannon on the GOP and the midterms: "We can't afford to lose"
summary: A key figure in President Trump's 2016 campaign and a former White House adviser, Steve Bannon remains an outspoken champion of the MAGA movement, who believes a Republican victory in the midterms is imperative.
story: There he was, in February 2017, on the cover of Time Magazine: Steve Bannon, chief White House strategist. They called him "The Great Manipulator." He threatened at times to overshadow the president himself – not the best career move – and for a while he visibly fell out of favor.

To this day, though, Bannon remains a passionate Trump supporter. "When Trump decides to leave the stage actively, he can't be replaced," he said. "Like Washington or Lincoln, these are people that they name the age of."

Yes, Bannon mentions Trump in the same breath as Washington and Lincoln. "Oh, I am," he said. "I think he's at that level. Because I think General Washington was there at the birth of the nation; Lincoln was the rebirth of the nation; and I absolutely believe (and I think 99% of MAGA believes) that Trump was there for the salvation of the nation."

Bannon is a man of unwavering commitment. He did four months in prison for contempt of Congress, for refusing to testify about his role in the events leading up to the January 6 assault on the U.S. Capitol (including telling podcast listeners on Jan. 5, 2021, "All hell is going to break loose tomorrow").
He set up an influential podcast, "War Room": Two hours in the morning, two hours in the evening. It was in his studio where, on September 29, we sat down for an interview.
Bannon clearly has a taste for the right wing. "Definitely, it's no doubt," he said. "I am right wing; I'm not conservative. I'm a right-winger and proud of it."

The Great Manipulator is, by most accounts, once again in regular and amicable communication with the president. But Bannon has no illusions. If Democrats gain control of the House in a couple of weeks, the "Age of MAGA" is in jeopardy. On his podcast he announced, "If we lose the House, it's going to turn the White House into Fort Apache."

Bannon told us what he sees as the repercussions of a Democratic victory: "I think you'll see Bobby Kennedy impeached, I'll think you see Pete Hegseth impeached. I think you'll see subpoenas flying every day. They will look to destroy President Trump, and we'll be bogged down for two years."

He believes that is a compelling argument to vote Republican this year – though polls show it may not be so compelling to the majority of American voters. "But you don't need the majority," Bannon argues. "Here's my point on the midterm: Remember, midterm elections are always driven by base getting out, and the base's ability to get more of their low-propensity voters out."

Bannon has few, if any, illusions about the agenda of old-line Republicans who are "all set for getting beyond Trump." But he disagrees that his own future lies beyond Trumpism. "First off, President Trump, I would say I'm the leader of trying to get President Trump to run for a third term," Bannon said. "It appears that he's not interested or it just won't happen."

He does not admit that the idea of a third term for Mr. Trump runs counter to the 22nd Amendment of the Constitution limiting a president to two terms. "Oh, I think you could drive a truck through that amendment," he said. "I talked to constitutional lawyers, and there were, I think, a number of different alternatives. Would it be contested? Yeah, it'd be contested, because everything [Trump] does is contested in the courts."
The war with Iran

The president is also confronting the same nemesis as his predecessor: old age. But Bannon does not see President Trump, who turned 80 this year, as having lost a step or two. "Oh, I don't agree with that," he said, claiming that the president works 20 hours a day. Nor does he dismiss the president's rambling speeches (such as his recent suggestion that Iran "take out" Los Angeles or San Diego).
"I would not call them 'drivel,'" Bannon said. "President Trump has been known to go off-script."

Any suggestion that Americans are embarrassed by Mr. Trump leads Bannon to draw accusations of media bias. "Ted, if you're part of the media elite, if you're a part of the East Coast elite, if you a Atlanticist, what President Trump has done, yes, you're not going to like it and probably you're going to hate it," he said. "I understand this war is a huge issue. But I think working-class Americans are not embarrassed. They're supportive of President Trump and how he presents the United States."

Despite polls that show a majority of Americans oppose the war with Iran, Bannon said, "Let's bifurcate the war. If you look at the first part, the 12-day war, and President Trump, the total obliteration of their nuclear program …"

Interrupted with the knowledge that Iran's nuclear capabilities have not been "totally" obliterated, Bannon replied, "I believe it's obliterated enough. What we're doing is tearing down their economy through economic warfare of Scott Bessant, given what he's doing with their currency, given the blockade on the oil."
The power of film

Interviewing Steve Bannon still offers the occasional surprise. If the Democratic Socialists sometimes offer positions that make more traditional Democratic candidate wince, count on Bannon to find hidden advantage for Republicans, while seeming to praise the opposition. "These people are very focused," he said. "Some of the candidates may stay way outside the mainstream, but they have a ground game that people have to understand that they have dedicated people and they're going to turn out their vote."

Bannon reminded me that he got into politics making films for the Tea Party: "I had a very particular take on it," he said. "It was very populist, very nationalistic. Critics came and said, 'Hey, this is fascist filmmaking.' And I said, 'Look, Leni Riefenstahl was one of the most powerful filmmakers ever.'"

Indeed, she was. Riefenstahl made the Nazis look mythical. Her coverage of military parades and the Berlin Olympics of 1936, in films such as "Triumph of the Will," has influenced filmmakers for decades, among them Bannon. In Alison Klayman's 2019 documentary "The Brink," Bannon was heard asking, "What would Leni Riefenstahl do? How would Leni cut that scene?

But most of all, Riefenstahl was known as Hitler's image-maker. "She was amoral, and she was a filmmaker for the Nazis, but her films were very powerful," said Bannon. "And what I was trying to do is to try to recreate the power of those films to make sure that people, particularly the little guy, understood that they could have a voice."

Over the past nine years Steve Bannon has cultivated ties with far-right movements across Europe. In March 2018, he spoke before the French National Front party's annual congress, telling Marine Le Pen and her followers, "You're part of a worldwide movement that is bigger than France, bigger than Italy, bigger than Hungary, bigger than all of it."

He is also close to Germany's fiercely anti-immigrant party, the AfD, which recently won a state election in a landslide. "Alternative for Deutschland is now here to teach us," he said. "They went to ground, and what they did is they went door-to-door, and they convinced people with no campaign money, that our way, our policies is to re-industrialize Germany, stop this mass immigration, re-migration, are policies you should vote for. I think we can learn a lot from them.
A question of fascism

Asked if the United States is moving toward fascism today, Bannon replied, "It's not fascism. It's actually more inclusionary, it's more entrepreneurial. It's not fascism at all. Remember if you go back, we win at the ballot box. The MAGA movement has only lost the Pelosi election of '18. The core belief of the MAGA movement is we won the 2020 election."
Except President Trump lost the 2020 election. "That's not true. We won!" Bannon exclaimed.
Actually, Joe Biden won. "It's not true," Bannon contested.

When faced with more than 60 court cases, all of which Mr. Trump lost while alleging election fraud, Bannon replied, "We can go debate this another time, but we didn't have standing. We never even got into court."

Bannon's technically correct; they didn't have standing. They couldn't find a judge who thought they had a significant case worth hearing. So, for six years they've just kept saying the same thing over and over.

But with the midterms upon us, Bannon was asked how he would bet on the outcome. "I would push all our chips in the middle of the table and say, 'Guys, there's no retreat, and there's no substitute for victory. Let's fight like hell,'" he said.

Is he suggesting that Republicans can't afford to lose? "Oh, we can't afford to lose. I don't think there's any doubt about that," he said – affirming that he will do whatever it takes to win the fight. "Exactly."

title: DOJ investigating TV networks over suspension of press pool after Trump media ban
summary: The Justice Department is investigating whether the major TV networks violated antitrust laws after they briefly suspended the TV press pool system in response to President Trump's decision to ban three news organizations from the White House.
story: The Justice Department is investigating whether the major TV networks, including CBS, violated antitrust laws after they briefly suspended the television press pool system in response to President Trump's decision last month to ban three news organizations from the White House.

"Members of the television press pool have boycotted covering White House events," Justice Department spokesperson Emily Covington said in a statement provided to CBS News on Saturday. "Group boycotts among commercial competitors can violate the Sherman Act. The Antitrust Division is simply investigating to determine whether these news organizations have violated the antitrust laws."

It was not immediately clear how the Justice Department was defining the move as a violation of the Sherman Act, which is a longstanding federal law that seeks to prevent monopolistic business behavior and maintain fair competition.
The New York Times was first to report the investigation. CBS News has reached out to the White House and all five networks — ABC, CBS, CNN, Fox and NBC — for comment.

In mid-September, Mr. Trump announced that his administration was rescinding the White House credentials of journalists for CNN, MSNOW and Politico over what he alleged was "their constant 'reporting' FAKE NEWS!"

The White House also sent letters to each of the three news outlets informing them that certain articles they had published on topics including the new White House ballroom, the ongoing war with Iran and the Republican midterm convention were threats to national security and violated standards of "professionalism and decorum" for reporters.

Following the move, the five networks that make up the TV press pool jointly announced that they would be suspending their coverage in solidarity. That suspension occurred at a critical moment in that it coincided with Chinese President Xi Jinping's state visit to Washington.

In a group statement at the time, the five networks said, "The public has a vital interest in receiving accurate, independent information about its government. No administration should reject a news organization because it objects to its reporting."
The TV press pool covers the president's travel and events on a rotating basis, providing video to other news organizations.

CNN, MSNOW and Politico immediately filed a lawsuit to have their access restored, and U.S. District Judge Timothy Kelly subsequently granted a temporary restraining order against the president's ban, and their credentials were reinstated.
However, despite having their credentials restored, the White House has continued to refuse to allow CNN and Politico into the Oval Office or aboard Air Force One.
That restraining order was set to expire on Thursday, but Kelly extended it to next Tuesday while he continues to consider the case.
CBS News and CNN are both part of Skydance, the parent company formed following the merger of Paramount and Warner Bros. Discovery that was finalized earlier this week.

title: SpaceX says Starlink will become a major U.S. mobile carrier
summary: SpaceX said it has bought licenses for radio airwaves that will help its Starlink satellite business provide cellphone service across the U.S.
story: Elon Musk's SpaceX has agreed to buy licenses for radio airwaves that will enable its Starlink Mobile satellite business to provide cellular service inside buildings, a move the company said will allow it to "become a major mobile carrier in the U.S."
"This is the last critical piece of the spectrum puzzle needed for SpaceX to provide complete phone coverage in America," Musk said in a social media post on Thursday.
SpaceX, a rocket developer and space exploration company, is buying the spectrum from investment firm Grain Management, according to a filing with the Federal Communications Commission.
Low-frequency radio spectrum can penetrate walls, overcoming an issue for Starlink's satellites, as walls, roofs and other structures can weaken mobile phone signals.

The spectrum purchase agreement, which still needs FCC approval, would allow Starlink to combine its satellite-to-mobile transmissions with "an advanced terrestrial deployment that can seamlessly connect devices everywhere," according to the company's statement.
SpaceX added that the FCC has approved Starlink Mobile's application to launch 15,000 satellites that will transmit radio waves in the 2 gigahertz band and connect directly to mobile phones.

"These airwaves are compatible with existing handsets, and we do not foresee obstacles to regulatory approval," UBS analyst John Hodulik said in a note to investors. "That said, we still believe it will take time for SpaceX to scale its wireless ambitions, and the impact to near-term wireless industry fundamentals is limited."

The announcement from SpaceX caused telecom companies' shares to tumble as investors considered the potential impact of a major new industry player. T-Mobile shares slid $18.58, or 11%, to $152.72 in morning trading on Friday, while AT&T slipped $1.83, or 7.4%, to $22.76.
Shares of SpaceX gained $2.61, or 1.6%, to $163.18.

title: Fort Hood shooter Nidal Hasan to be executed Dec. 3, email states
summary: Nidal Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961.
story: An execution date for former Army Maj. Nidal Hasan, who killed 13 people in a 2009 shooting at Fort Hood, has been set for Dec. 3, 2026, and will take place at the same post where he carried out his attack, according to an email sent to the families of victims.
Hasan is set to die by firing squad in what will be the first military execution since 1961.
Pentagon spokesman Sean Parnell said late Monday that the plan to use an Army firing squad was recommended by Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth and approved by President Trump.
"Judgement day for Hasan has finally come," Parnell wrote.
CBS Texas has reached out to Fort Hood for comment and was directed to Army headquarters.

In addition to the 13 people Hasan killed on Nov. 5, 2009, 32 others were injured. Those targeted were unarmed soldiers who were at the readiness center as they were preparing to deploy. Hasan fired 146 times.
The last military execution took place 65 years ago, when the Army executed Pvt. John Bennett by hanging after he was convicted of rape and the attempted murder of an 11-year-old girl.
The last execution by firing squad happened during World War II, when Pvt. Eddie Slovik was put to death in France for desertion.

Hasan, now 56, was an Army psychiatrist at the time of the shootings. He had served two decades in the Army. Witnesses described hearing Hasan shout "Allahu Akbar" before opening fire. Hasan was paralyzed from the chest down when police returned fire.
Since his conviction, Hasan has been on death row at Fort Leavenworth in Kansas.
Why a firing squad?

According to Army regulation 190-55, military executions can only be approved by the president. A 2019 revision removed the term "lethal injection" from this regulation and left the method up to the secretary of the Army's designation. According to the guidelines, the method is recommended to the secretary by the provost marshal general.

According to this order, the prisoner is informed of the president's decision in person by the commandant, who is accompanied by a chaplain and, if available, a defense attorney. After the notification, the prisoner becomes a "condemned prisoner."
The victims

Family members of those who died were notified of the planned execution before the announcement was made. They, along with survivors, were asked if they wanted to attend. The group, bonded in tragedy, has been intertwined over the last 17 years. This is what many hope will be the final chapter in the tragedy.

title: Hackers heat up refrigerators at hundreds of supermarkets: "Unprecedented"
summary: The cyberattack caused refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, sparking fires and forcing spoiled food to be thrown away.
story: Major French supermarket chains on Monday said they were hit by a cyberattack that caused their refrigerators to shoot up in temperature in hundreds of stores, forcing spoiled food to be thrown away and raising concerns about food security.
Top retailers E. Leclerc, Intermarché and Cooperative U confirmed to AFP they suffered a cyberattack that Cooperative U's chief executive described as "unprecedented."

"Food security requires more attention at all levels," said the EU's food and agriculture commissioner Christophe Hansen on X, condemning the attack and saying such "exploitation of food" was now a "reality."
At least 300 shops of Intermarché or its Netto brand were targeted, along with over 100 Cooperative U outlets, and several E. Leclerc stores, the retailers told AFP in separate statements.

"Targeting equipment essential to the preservation of fresh products and to the food supply of the French people is of extreme gravity and is unprecedented," Cooperative U CEO Dominique Schelcher wrote on X.
Paris prosecutors confirmed the attack, which reportedly also hit other major chains, and also indicated it had sparked fires.
BFM TV said hackers "managed to remotely trigger the forced defrosting of the refrigeration systems in numerous stores."
The affected branches will have to "throw away all of the products" that are fresh and frozen, Intermarché told AFP.
Carrefour said 80 of its supermarkets were attacked but that the vast majority of its 6,000 stores were not affected, according to the Reuters news agency.
E. Leclerc confirmed to AFP "that a cyberattack affected one of its refrigeration equipment suppliers," resulting in "repercussions on the operation of refrigeration systems in several stores."
A source close to the issue said refrigeration control systems from Danish manufacturer Danfoss were targeted.
Danfoss told AFP in a statement that most of the affected equipment was "legacy" products which "no longer receive software or security updates."

It said its AK-SM800 and AK-SC355 fridge regulator systems were notably affected, with a version of the former using "outdated firmware." It added that it had long advised supermarkets to update from those models. Danfoss gave no figures on how many systems were affected.

Dutch supermarket operator Ahold Delhaize, which also has operations in the United States, said it was also dealing with a "security issue" in its network, Reuters reported. A phone app for the retailer told clients that due to a "cybersecurity incident" it was unable to deliver groceries.
"Large-scale cyberattack"

A person close to French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said France's cybersecurity agency had already identified "a vulnerability in software supplied by a Danish company and has contacted the vendor."

"It is liaising with its European counterparts, as other countries may be affected," and is seeking "to identify other French companies involved in order to alert them" and "prevent the spread," the source added.

The office of the Paris prosecutor confirmed to AFP that an investigation has been opened into "the large-scale cyberattack affecting the refrigerators of several major food retail chains across France."
The probe will help "identify the victims and establish the link with the damage they reported in terms of foodstuff losses and the outbreak of fires," the prosecutor's office said.
Intermarché condemned the food waste and financial losses resulting from the attack, without providing figures.
BFM TV said temperatures were "altered remotely, resulting in the destruction of stocks of fresh and frozen products."
Rising fears of hybrid attacks
The incident comes against the background of growing concern over the potential havoc that can be caused in Europe in all sectors by malicious actors carrying out cyberattacks.

President Emmanuel Macron, a strong supporter of Ukraine in its fight against the Russian invasion, last month ordered measures to protect France's critical infrastructure from Russian "hybrid attacks."

Industrial equipment such as refrigeration units, long isolated from the internet, is now connected via sensors or remote monitoring systems, Antoine Hautin of cybersecurity consultancy Almond told AFP.
By likely affecting hundreds of units simultaneously, the attack demonstrated "a certain level of sophistication," he added.

title: Pope Leo to go to hospital Tuesday for lung nodule surgery
summary: Pope Leo XIV​ revealed the discovery of a lung nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors' advice to have it removed.
story: Pope Leo XIV will be admitted to the hospital on Tuesday, days after he shared he would undergo surgery to remove a lung nodule discovered during recent medical tests, the Vatican announced.
The Holy See press office didn't say when the operation itself would take place, but said it will require a weeklong recovery in the hospital.
The U.S.-born pontiff revealed the discovery of the nodule during his Sunday noon prayer and said he was following doctors' advice to have it removed.
He said it was found in an early stage and was "circumscribed."

"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo, 71, said Sunday. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."
He will be treated at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which has a special apartment for the pope.
The Vatican press office said Monday that no particular issue precipitated the tests, denying Italian media reports suggesting an inflammation had prompted Leo to undergo the checkup.

The pope's surgery marks the first major health event of his 17-month pontificate. It was significant because the pope himself revealed the news, in perhaps the most public way possible: at the end of his Sunday noon blessing with thousands of people in St. Peter's Square.

The Vatican has for centuries zealously guarded the pope's health and has often sent out confusing information, or none at all, about papal illnesses. Pope Francis tried to change that by being upfront about his frailties and musing on his eventual death. But even during his pontificate, information was tightly controlled.
Leo's decision and reveal suggested an unusual level of transparency by the American pope.

A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1 inch that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.

On Monday, it was business as usual at the Vatican. Leo presided over an audience with members of a Rome-based charity, the Circolo San Pietro, and received a donation from them. He spoke in a strong, clear voice, praising their service and sacrifice. The crowd gave him a rousing round of applause afterward.

He had six other private audiences, made three appointments and the Vatican released a letter he had penned to the outgoing dean of the College of Cardinals, thanking him for his service. The letter was signed on Sunday.
In the afternoon, he was expected to continue his audiences and, if time, rejoin a weeklong conference he convened on ministering to families.
The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary.

title: Hurricane Simon lashes Mexico's Pacific coast, pounds resorts and towns
summary: Although Simon weakened on Monday, the hurricane continued to pound vulnerable parts of Mexico's Pacific Coast.
story: Hurricane Simon weakened Monday to a Category 2 storm, but it continued to pound the coast of west-central Mexico as its eye remained just offshore.

Dangerous winds were expected to keep lashing the region through the morning, threatening coastal areas with flooding rain, said the U.S. National Hurricane Center. With its center still swirling parallel to the coast, Simon's most damaging winds and rain were forecast to persist near the Puerto Vallarta area, a coastal town known for its beach resorts.

The storm's maximum sustained winds have decreased to 110 mph, dipping just below the 111 mph needed to make it a major Category 3 storm, according to the hurricane center. Simon had been weakening gradually since the early hours of Monday morning, local time, but forecasters warned that it could strengthen again, and, regardless, it remained a dangerous hurricane.

As of the hurricane center's latest update, Simon was moving slowly northwestward off the Mexican coast. But the storm was expected to change directions mid-week, and eventually approach the coast of west-central Mexico on Wednesday into Thursday.

"Some additional weakening is forecast today, but Simon could re-intensify some on Tuesday and Wednesday and is expected to remain a hurricane through midweek," the center said Monday. "Rapid weakening is likely after Simon moves inland late this week."

Puerto Vallarta is a popular tourist destination in the state of Jalisco. Just inland and uphill from the resort areas, many Mexicans live in communities where housing might not stand up to the storm.

Simon is expected to bring heavy rain to the U.S Southern Plains from Tuesday afternoon through Friday morning, CBS News and Stations Meteorologist Nikki Nolan points out. That region could see 3 to 5 inches of rain and more in some places.
Early Monday, Simon's eye was about 55 miles west-southwest of Cabo Corrientes and moving northwest at about 3 mph.

A senior hurricane center specialist, Philippe Papin, said the westernmost tip of mainland Mexico is the area most likely to get a direct hit from the system. Cabo Corrientes is at the southern tip of Bahia de Banderas, the wide bay where Puerto Vallarta looks out to the Pacific.

Hurricane-force winds were extending outward up to 15 miles and tropical-storm-force winds were reaching up to 60 miles from Simon's center, meaning the entire area between Mexico's western coast and the Sierra Madre mountains could be affected.

"We're expecting catastrophic wind and life-threatening storm surge impacts along that west-central coast of Mexico where the hurricane warning is currently in effect," Papin said. "They're also getting very heavy rainfall associated with the storm that's likely going to produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides in areas of higher terrain along the Mexican coastline, and there will be significant swells."

The hurricane center said early Monday that Simon was expected to dump an additional 2 to 4 inches of rain, with some areas getting up to 8 inches, in the states of Colima, Jalisco, Nayarit and Sinaloa through early Thursday.

"Isolated maximum storm totals of 30 inches are possible over portions of the states of Michoacan, Colima, and Jalisco," the center said in its latest advisory. "This rainfall will produce life-threatening flooding and mudslides or worsen any ongoing flooding, especially in areas of steep terrain."

As the storm approached Puerto Vallarta, National Guard vehicles patrolled the streets while police used a megaphone to call out the few people who were jogging, walking their dogs or biking by the waterfront. Officers reminded people that the area was closed and urged them to take shelter. Not everyone followed the orders.

Jalisco state suspended classes on Friday and Monday in 22 coastal municipalities and began evacuating people from at-risk areas while asking the tourism sector to make sure workers and visitors are fully accommodated in shelters or safe zones.

Mexican President Claudia Sheinbaum took to social media to urge people in Jalisco, Colima, Nayarit and Michoacan to stay sheltered until the government issues a notification that the danger has passed. She also asked people to follow recommendations from civil protection officials and to avoid traveling on public roads.
"Precautionary evacuation efforts to safe zones are ongoing; the priority is our safety," she wrote.

Hotel worker Víctor Martínez went shopping for nonperishable food Sunday afternoon. He said he couldn't go to work because public transportation service was suspended and most of the hotel had been evacuated.
Martínez found people's concerns about the hurricane comforting.

"It happened to us before. It hit us years ago," Martínez said, referring to a Category 5 hurricane that hit the area in 2002. "People didn't expect it. We were very skeptical that it would ever hit us. Now, though, we're different. Precautions are being taken. It happened to us once, and we won't let it happen again."
Despite the risks posed by Simon, tourists were still arriving in Puerto Vallarta.

Visitors Ricardo Ramírez and Brenda Villarreal, who have never lived through a hurricane, went looking for food by the city's boardwalk and came across police urging people to take shelter. Ramírez said they were completely unprepared for the situation.
"The boardwalk is closed. Be responsible. Understand!" police told passersby using a megaphone.
Ramírez said he and Villarreal had planned their four-day vacation since last year and traveled from Guadalajara, Jalisco's capital.
"We don't know the extent of the danger yet," Villarreal said. "We're just starting to see what's going on."

Unlike the Atlantic, which saw just its first named hurricane of the season this week with Isaias, the Pacific season has been very active. Simon's arrival comes on the heels of Polo, which slammed Mexico last week as a Category 2 hurricane before reaching the southwestern U.S. and bringing heavy flooding to the region.

title: Stolen Renoir paintings found hidden behind cinder block wall
summary: Thieves broke into the museum and escaped with two works by Renoir, abandoning two others as they fled. The value of all four paintings was estimated at $10 million.
story: Two paintings by impressionist master Pierre-Auguste Renoir, stolen from a museum in southern France and later discovered hidden behind a wall, have sustained slight damage, prosecutors said on Monday.
In September, thieves broke into the museum in Cagnes-sur-Mer and escaped with two works by Renoir, abandoning two others as they fled.
The value of all four paintings had been estimated at $10 million.
On Friday, authorities announced that the two outstanding stolen works had been found.
They were a portrait titled "Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano" and a depiction of a woman at a well called "Young Woman at the Well."
Speaking to reporters in Paris, Marseille prosecutor Nicolas Bessone said the paintings were recovered last Thursday during a search of a home in the southern town of Clermont-l'Herault.
The discovery of the stolen works followed the arrest of six people, including a woman, last Wednesday, said Bessone.

"The paintings were hidden behind a solid cinder block wall. They were completely undetectable," Bessone said. "It was through interrogation work that investigators were able to get the receiver of the stolen goods to admit that he had indeed taken possession of the paintings."
A 29-year-old man seen as the main suspect was charged over the weekend after DNA evidence linked him to the theft.

The two paintings were "in relatively good condition," although "the two works showed signs of damage," Bessone said, speaking alongside the head of France's national judicial police, Christian Sainte.
The frame of "Young Woman at the Well" was slightly damaged, while "the canvas of 'Portrait of Madame Colonna Romano' had a tear," Bessone said.
The tear was located "on the dress" in the portrait, the prosecutor said, adding that both paintings "will require restoration work."
String of recent heists
Culture Minister Catherine Pegard praised "the efficiency and determination of all those who made this outcome possible."
"Their commitment made it possible to recover these works in record time," the culture ministry said.
A spate of heists at French museums — including at the Louvre — has highlighted inadequate security in some cases and led to questions about whether criminal gangs see them as soft targets.
Crown jewels valued at around $100 million were stolen in broad daylight from the Louvre in Paris last year.
The suspected thieves have been arrested and charged, but none of the jewels have been recovered except for a crown that was dropped as the group escaped.
Other French museums have been targeted in recent months. In July, burglars stole millions of dollars worth of jewelry from the museum of French luxury glassmaker Lalique.
In October 2025, a woman was arrested and charged over the theft of gold from the Natural History Museum in Paris.

The month before that, thieves snatched three porcelain works worth millions of dollars and classed as national treasures in a heist at the Adrien Dubouche National Museum in Limoges in central France.

title: Russell Brand goes on trial to face rape and sexual assault charges
summary: British actor Russell Brand​ has appeared in a London court for the start of his trial on rape and sexual assault charges.
story: London — British comedian and actor Russell Brand appeared in a London court on Monday for the start of his trial on rape and sexual assault charges.
The hearing at Southwark Crown Court was adjourned until Tuesday after a morning of jury selection. The prosecution is due to open its case later in the week.

Brand, who is on bail, left the court building beside the River Thames holding hands with his wife, Laura Gallacher. He had earlier arrived at court flanked by security guards and accompanied by his wife.

Brand, 51, has pleaded not guilty to three counts of rape, three counts of sexual assault and one count of indecent assault. The charges involve six women and alleged offenses between 1999 and 2009. The trial is expected to last up to 10 weeks.

Prosecutors said at previous hearings that Brand is accused of raping a woman in a hotel room at a Labour Party conference, grabbing a TV worker's breasts and forcing her into a sex act in a toilet, and kissing and groping a radio station worker.

Known for risque stand-up routines and battles with drugs and alcohol, Brand rose to prominence in the early 2000s, hosting television programs and his own BBC radio show. He appeared in Hollywood films including "Forgetting Sarah Marshall" and "Get Him to the Greek."

In recent years he has moved away from mainstream media, relocated to Florida and built a large online following with videos mixing wellness, conspiracy theories and discussions of his religious devotion.
The Associated Press doesn't name victims of alleged sexual violence, and British law protects their identities from the media for life.

title: 139 people dead, including 15 children, after migrant boat capsizes
summary: "What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," a U.N. official said.
story: At least 139 people, including children, have died after a boat carrying more than 300 migrants capsized off the coast of Djibouti in east Africa, the International Organization for Migration said Sunday.

"This is a devastating loss of life. Our thoughts are with the survivors and the families who have lost loved ones or remain without news of their relatives," Alexandre Coissac, IOM chief of mission in Djibouti, said in a statement.

That number only includes those buried by authorities in Djibouti. Others have been buried by the migrants themselves, but they won't be added to the official count until authorities can verify the bodies, Coissac told the AP via the phone.
"What is terrible is that they were buried with no names, in a common grave, like in a war situation," Coissac said. "They all have a mother, a father, and we may never learn what happened."
Coissac said the migrants boarded the ship in the evening of Oct. 8 and that it sank very soon after, close to the shore, "mainly because it was overcrowded."
"The local authorities did their best," Coissac said, "but they were overwhelmed with all the bodies that kept coming at once towards the shore."

The IOM said among the bodies recovered were nine girls and six boys. More than 80 people survived the shipwreck, all Ethiopian nationals. IOM released video of the aftermath of the wreck, showing the capsized vessel and victims' clothes on the shore.
He said authorities were bringing the surviving migrants to the IOM rescue center in Obock where they receive medical assistance after swallowing sea water, and psychological support.
"They're all in a state of shock," said Coissac, who visited the area of the shipwreck Saturday. "I tried to talk to some of them but it's very difficult."

Some of the migrants in the IOM center are already aware that their family members died during the shipwreck. Others were given access to phones to call loved ones back home to notify them they are alive.

At least 84 people remained missing in one of the deadliest shipwrecks yet on the popular but perilous crossing from the Horn of Africa to the Arabian Peninsula, where many migrants seek work in rich Gulf nations.
The boat was traveling from Djibouti to Yemen when it capsized on Thursday night or Friday morning, according to the IOM. More than 80 people survived, all of them Ethiopian nationals, it said.
The Geneva-based U.N. migration agency said the vessel had 305 people on board and warned that the death toll could still rise.
Personal items likely belonging to the migrants, including shoes, were seen on a beach in a video shared by IOM. Rescue work continued as fears grew for the missing.

Tens of thousands of migrants from the Horn of Africa travel every year through Djibouti and across the Bab el-Mandeb Strait toward Gulf countries in search of safety and economic opportunities, the IOM said in its statement.
That movement has continued despite newly escalating fighting in Yemen, on the other side of the strait.
"This is a devastating loss of life," said Coissac. "This tragedy is a stark reminder of the dangers faced by migrants along this migration corridor as they seek economic opportunities."

In recent weeks, at least 2,000 Yemenis have received aid in Djibouti as the fighting has escalated in Yemen between the Saudi-backed, internationally recognized government and Iranian-backed Houthi rebels.

That's the opposite direction from the movement of the migrants who died in the shipwreck and the typical migration patterns of recent years: The tens of thousands who cross from eastern Africa toward Yemen each year have typically been looking for work in places like Saudi Arabia.
More than 900 migrants died or went missing along the route last year, according to IOM's Missing Migrants Project, while the number undertaking the journey increased by 18%.
Earlier this year, IOM said 53 people were dead or missing after a boat capsized in the Mediterranean Sea off the Libyan coast. Only two survivors were rescued.

"No one gets into a boat like that unless they believe there is no other safe way," IOM Director-General Amy Pope said. "We cannot keep treating these deaths as normal. Safe and legal pathways save lives. I am asking governments and donors to act before the next boat goes down."

title: Saudi airport hit again, a day after deadly strike killed 13
summary: The strike on King Khalid International Airport, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom.
story: One person was killed after a passenger terminal at the international airport in Riyadh, Saudi Arabia, was attacked again on Sunday, a day after a deadly strike on the Riyadh airport killed 13 people, including a U.S. citizen, and wounded hundreds of others.
The second attack comes as Yemen's Houthi group said they carried out at least four operations targeting King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh since Saturday.

Saudi authorities said there were injuries in the latest attack on the King Khalid International Airport complex for terminals 3 and 4, serving domestic flights. The airport — struck four times in the past five days — has been closed since Saturday's missile attack, which was the deadliest in a Gulf Arab nation since the Iran war began. Over 300 other people were wounded, some critically.

Houthi military spokesman Brig. Gen. Yahya Saree said on Telegram that the attacks are in response to "brutal Saudi aggression against our country and our people," CBS News partner BBC News reported. He claimed Saudi Arabia launched more than 120 airstrikes in the past 24 hours in Houthi-controlled territory in Yemen.

The Houthis said their other targets included the Shugadam gas facility, which belongs to Saudi's national petroleum and natural gas company Aramco, the Tanajib oil refinery, and King Fahd International Airport in Dammam, the BBC reported.
Saudi's civil aviation authority confirmed the strike on King Fahd Airport.

Saturday's strike at the airport, the deadliest on Saudi soil in more than a decade, marked a major escalation in the war between Yemen's Iran-backed Houthis and the kingdom and further complicated sputtering efforts to halt the U.S.-Iran war.

Saudi Arabia has moved Riyadh schools online amid the Houthis' latest threat. Flights were diverted elsewhere, the Flightradar24 tracker said. Countries including the U.S., Britain, Germany, Australia and Canada warned citizens to avoid the airport.
Earlier on Saturday, the Houthies threatened new attacks on the kingdom's airports, except for the holy sites of Mecca and Medina, warning passengers not to travel.
"The airports and airspace are exposed to targeting and constitute a theatre of operations for our forces," Saree wrote on X.
He urged "everyone to take our warnings seriously."
On Sunday, the Houthis said the airport under their control in the Yemeni capital of Sanaa had been struck again. They blamed the Saudis but provided no details.
The attack on Riyadh's airport on Saturday drew condemnation from the United Nations and world leaders, including President Trump, who said he was considering joining Saudi strikes on the Houthis.

"The United States strongly condemns the recent attacks on the Kingdom of Saudi Arabia by the terrorist Houthis, including today's strike on King Khalid International Airport in Riyadh that took numerous innocent lives, including an American citizen," Secretary of State Marco Rubio said in a social media post.
A State Department spokesperson told CBS News the Trump administration is in close contact with its "Saudi partners."
European Commission President Ursula von der Leyen said the attacks by Iran's proxies are "pushing the region into a spiral of violence."
"They are destabilizing crucial global transport and energy nodes," she wrote on X.
Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu on Sunday condemned "in the strongest possible terms" the attack on King Khalid Airport and extended his condolences.

"Terrorism targets innocent people and seeks to spread fear and instability. It must be confronted with resolve," he said in a statement shared on X. "Israel looks forward to a strong Middle East—one that stands united against threats, protects its people, and builds a future of security, cooperation, and prosperity for all the peoples of our region.

The Saudi statement about Saturday's attack said the dead included four Saudi citizens, two Bangladeshi nationals, a Palestinian, a U.S. citizen, an Egyptian, a Jordanian, a Syrian and a Sudanese. It said several hospitals were treating the 309 people injured, some in serious condition.
The Egyptian woman was a flight attendant identified as Azza Ramzy, 28, who worked for the Saudi airline Flynas, according to the Egyptian state-run Al-Qahera News television.
The Indian embassy in Saudi Arabia said Sunday that one of its citizens died after being wounded in the attack on the Riyadh airport a day earlier.

"It is learnt that one Indian national injured in the Riyadh attack has unfortunately lost his life today. We convey our heartfelt condolences to the family of the deceased," the embassy wrote in a statement posted on X.
The Houthis claimed attacks earlier in the week on King Khalid International Airport that killed three Saudis, including a pilot. The airport has no military facilities.

The surge in attacks, including against other Saudi airports, military facilities and oil infrastructure, has come in the week since a Saudi-led coalition launched a major military offensive against the Houthis.

title: Pope Leo to undergo surgery after nodular lesion found in lung, Vatican says
summary: The American pope has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active
story: Pope Leo XIV will undergo surgery this week after a nodular lesion was found in his lung, the Vatican said. Recovery is expected to take a week.
Leo, 71, said Sunday that doctors recently discovered the nodular lesion during medical checks. He said it was found in an early stage and was "circumscribed."

"The doctors believe it's best to take action, so, following their advice, I've decided to have surgery to remove it," Leo said in remarks during his Sunday noon blessing. "Thank you for your spiritual support, and I entrust myself to your prayers."
A statement by Vatican spokesperson Matteo Bruni didn't say when the pope would be hospitalized but that it would be in the "first days" of the week.
The Vatican said Monday that the pontiff is maintaining his regular schedule for the day as he awaits the surgery, according to the Reuters news service.
He was expected to be treated at Rome's Gemelli Hospital, which has a special apartment for the pope.

A lung nodule is a small abnormal area measuring less than 1 inch that sometimes appears on a CT scan of the chest or abdomen, according to the American Cancer Society. Often, the scans are done to investigate trauma or a lung infection, unrelated to a lung cancer screening.

"Lung nodules are fairly common and are often benign, but benign and cancerous nodules can have a similar appearance on imaging," said Dr. Stephen Liu, a lung cancer expert at Georgetown's Lombardi Comprehensive Cancer Center.

"When there is sufficient concern, and when it is safe to do so based on the location of the nodule and the overall health of the patient, surgical removal can provide a definitive diagnosis," he said in an email.

The pope has a major trip planned Nov. 6-17 to Uruguay, Argentina and Peru. It's unclear whether the planned surgery and recovery would affect the itinerary, but Leo said earlier in his remarks Sunday that he planned to go.

The American pope has no previously known health problems and is known to be physically active, with weekly tennis games and swimming at the papal summer retreat in Castel Gandolfo. This, Dr. Massimo Di Maio, president of the Italian Association of Medical Oncology, said, is "an important starting point for coping as well as possible with treatment, including surgery."

Di Maio said it will be important to determine if the nodule is benign or malignant, and if it is malignant, whether it has spread. When the disease is detected at an early stage, "the aim … is curative," he added.
Depending on what is found, possible treatments can include chemotherapy and radiation therapy, Di Maio told Italy's private Sky TG24.

"When we talk about something being localized, that can also refer to the need to establish whether the disease is confined to that one site or whether scans show signs of disease elsewhere," he said, adding that he has not treated the pope and was speaking about the disease in general.

Leo's predecessor, Pope Francis, died April 21, 2025, of a stroke following a long hospitalization brought on by a respiratory crisis that developed into double pneumonia. Francis suffered from chronic lung disease and had part of one lung removed as a young man.
