title: Grandmother of 12 holds plank for 5 hours in record-breaking feat
summary: DonnaJean Wilde held an abdominal plank for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games, smashing her own Guinness world record by nearly 30 minutes.
story: DonnaJean Wilde broke the female abdominal plank world record after holding the position for five hours at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah and beating her previous time by nearly 30 minutes.
A 61-year-old Canadian grandmother broke the female abdominal plank world record after holding the position for five hours.
DonnaJean Wilde accomplished the feat at the Huntsman World Senior Games in Utah on Oct. 4, breaking her own record by nearly 30 minutes, Storyful reported.
Wilde’s plank began at 3:03 p.m. and ended at 8:03 p.m., with several judges rotating in and out of shifts during that period, a spokesperson for the World Senior Games told Storyful.
FITNESS INFLUENCER SAYS ONE SIMPLE HABIT CAN HELP ANYONE GET BACK IN SHAPE

Her previous record of 4 hours, 30 minutes and 11 seconds was set on March 21, 2004, at the Canadian high school where she once served as vice principal, according to the Guinness Book of World Records.
"To successfully achieve the record, the challenger’s forearms and toes must touch the ground at all times," Guinness states.
The feat occurred at the Huntsman World Senior Games Oct. 4 in Utah, where DonnaJean Wilde broke her own record by nearly 30 minutes, according to Storyful. (WorldSeniorGames via Storyful)
"The remainder of the body must be lifted off the ground and be kept straight throughout," it also says.
FITNESS EXPERT REVEALS 6 THINGS PEOPLE OVER 35 SHOULD DO AFTER WORKOUTS TO STAY STRONG
"My elbows hurt pretty bad," Wilde said after completing the previous record.
"I was so worried about losing my form, and I think that’s why my quads hurt because I was just really tense."
A woman in her early 60s has broken her own planking record by nearly 30 minutes. (iStock)
She shared with Guinness that the first two hours "went by quickly," but the next two hours were much more difficult.
"The last hour was the most challenging, just to stay focused and keep my form," she said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
During the last 30 minutes, she said she focused on "breathing, staying calm and not shaking."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Wilde first added planking to her daily routine years ago after breaking her wrist because she could perform the exercise while wearing a cast.
"I realized that I could read and do things when I was planking and fell in love with it," she said, according to the report.
Wilde shared some advice for others aiming to hold extended planks.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
"Keep trying and keep practicing. When you have to read or work on your computer, just get on the floor and do it on the floor."
Wilde has 12 grandchildren, according to Guinness.

Her new record is pending review and approval by Guinness.

title: Doctor reveals 4 hidden health risks of spending too much time indoors
summary: A Nature & Health Alliance survey finds nearly half of Americans spend under two hours outdoors weekly, fueling burnout, brain fog and belly fat.
story: Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and expert in nature-based medicine, discusses how humans spend about 93% of their lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax."
Nearly half of Americans spend less than two hours outdoors in an entire week, according to a new national survey from the Nature & Health Alliance involving researchers at Texas A&M University.
Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and expert in nature-based medicine, has focused on the potential health impacts of spending less time outdoors.
In his book, "Indoor Epidemic," he discusses how humans spend about 93% of their lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax." He claims the remedy is a simple 7% outdoor prescription.
NEARLY 3 IN 4 AMERICANS ARE BATTLING THE SAME EXHAUSTING HEALTH PROBLEM, CDC REVEALS

"Many people don't realize that they're inhibited from feeling as good as they can, because they're exhausted even after a full night's sleep," La Puma told Fox News Digital. "They need coffee to feel normal. They crash at 2 in the afternoon. They're wired at night. They can't go to sleep, but their labs are normal."
"And they come into the office saying, ‘Why do I feel so exhausted?’ It's the four Bs," he said.
Nearly half of Americans spend less than two hours outdoors in an entire week, according to a new national survey. (iStock)
The ‘4 Bs’ caused by too much indoor time
Outdoor light can be many times brighter than typical indoor lighting, La Puma noted, making it a powerful signal for setting the body’s internal clock, or circadian rhythm.
"If you don't set your body clock, your body doesn't know what time it is, and it just goes to sleep whenever you can get to sleep instead of on time," he told Fox News Digital.
Dr. John La Puma, a California physician and author of "Indoor Epidemic," has focused on the potential health impacts of spending less time outdoors. (John La Puma)
SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISINGLY EASY EXERCISE THAT MAY BOOST YOUR MOOD IN JUST 10 MINUTES
Getting bright outdoor light soon after waking can help synchronize the body's sleep-wake cycle and support the natural rise in melatonin later in the evening, according to La Puma.
He recommends spending about 10 minutes outdoors within the first hour of waking, without sunglasses.
La Puma uses the term "ultraprocessed time" to describe hours lost to screens, scrolling and other digital distractions.
"Ultraprocessed time is kind of like ultraprocessed food," he said. "It’s not nutritious. It’s synthetic. It’s artificial. It’s ubiquitous."
The doctor discusses how humans spend about 93% of our lives inside, which comes with a "hidden health tax." He claims that a simple 7% outdoor prescription can fix it. (iStock)
That includes time spent endlessly scrolling, he said, which can seem to simply "evaporate."
La Puma argues that a person’s environment can contribute to burnout, rather than viewing it solely as a matter of willpower.
AMERICA'S NATIONAL PARKS COULD ADD YEARS TO YOUR LIFE — HERE'S HOW THEY BOOST HEALTH

Spending excessive time indoors can lead to an overload of screen exposure, he said, as people often turn to the same devices for work, entertainment and relaxation. He noted that the body may not interpret screen time as true rest or escape.
"And equally important, no horizon. We are horizon-deprived as a species because indoors, we can't see more than 20 feet in front of us," La Puma said.
"Your eyes need distance like your lungs need air."
To combat burnout, he recommends getting up and going to the window and looking outside for a minute every hour.

"It relaxes your eyes, relaxes the muscles around your temples, reduces headache if you have it, improves energy and reduces fatigue," he said. "That's the beginning of being able to reverse burnout."
DOCTORS SAY 8 FORGOTTEN HABITS COULD HELP FIGHT STRESS, OBESITY AND CHRONIC DISEASE
Simply going outside during the workday can help to reverse burnout, LaPuma said.
"Your eyes need distance like your lungs need air."
People who spend the day indoors may notice that they feel mentally foggy by the afternoon, La Puma said, particularly in poorly ventilated spaces where carbon dioxide can build up.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Indoor CO₂ levels can climb above 1,000 parts per million in poorly ventilated spaces, and some research has linked elevated levels with reduced cognitive performance.
"So it's not that you're just making bad decisions in the afternoons — there's a biologic reason for it," La Puma said.
People who spend the day indoors may notice that they feel mentally foggy by the afternoon, the doctor said. (iStock)
"What you need to do is cross-ventilate, but that's tough to do in an office or conference room."

The doctor said that getting outdoors gives the eyes a chance to focus at greater distances while providing a break from potentially stuffy indoor air. The EPA notes that concentrations of some pollutants can be two to five times higher indoors than outdoors.
When someone’s body clock is out of sync, it can disrupt the body’s normal cortisol rhythm, La Puma said.

Cortisol, often called the stress hormone, naturally rises and falls throughout the day. Research has linked altered cortisol activity with greater abdominal and visceral fat, although the relationship is complex.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Again, the way to improve your metabolism is to get daylight at the right time, in the right place, for the right duration — early in the morning especially," La Puma advised.
"This will give you a bump in cortisol, which you want early in the morning to feel awake, and then it drops appropriately."
The 17-minute dose
Most people spend about an hour outdoors each day as they walk from the car to the office, for example — but that's what La Puma calls "incidental time," not "biologically active time."
"Be intentional with your time — look at the sky in the morning when you have your 10 minutes outdoors to reset your body clock and watch the clouds," the doctor advised. (iStock)
To combat the four Bs, he recommends spending "intentional time" outdoors, "in a blue or green space," for a minimum effective dose of 17 minutes a day.
"Be intentional with your time — look at the sky in the morning … to reset your body clock and watch the clouds," the doctor advised.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

For those who live in a big city and can’t see the sky, La Puma recommends looking at a distant rooftop, or looking through an open window when going outside isn’t possible. The goal is to focus beyond the confines of an indoor space.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"So 17 minutes a day is the minimum effective dose — that's all it takes to begin to bend the curve on the four Bs," he said.
"You can turn those minutes into medicine."

title: Diet soda vs water: Study reveals which beverage is better for weight loss
summary: A two-year randomized trial found that diet drinks with aspartame, sucralose and acesulfame potassium matched water for weight loss outcomes.
story: Pop’s Social co-founders Sam Sachs and Ali Greenberg demonstrate how to make a dirty soda on ‘Fox & Friends Weekend.’
Diet drinks containing sugar substitutes were found to be as effective as water for supporting weight loss in overweight or obese adults, according to a two-year randomized trial.
The study, led by the University of Liverpool, England, included 493 participants ranging from 18 to 65 years old, all of whom had a body mass index (BMI) between 27 and 35 (overweight or obese).
Half of them received 22.3 ounces of water each day, and the other half received the same amount of soda with non-nutritive sweeteners (about two cans) for a 104-week period.
YOUR BRAIN MAY BE TRICKING YOU INTO LIKING ARTIFICIAL SWEETENERS, STUDY FINDS

The group assigned to NNS drinks could choose from a variety of diet sodas, low-calorie fruit drinks and flavored waters. The primary sweeteners used were aspartame, acesulfame potassium and sucralose.
After two years, people drinking diet beverages had lost about 10.6 pounds, while those drinking water lost about 8.2 pounds.
Diet drinks containing sugar substitutes were found to be as effective as water for supporting weight loss in overweight or obese adults, according to a two-year randomized trial. (iStock)
People in both groups kept off a meaningful amount of weight for two years, even during the last year when they no longer had regular weight-management support, the researchers stated.
Both groups lost inches around their waists and hips and reduced body fat, but there was no meaningful difference between people drinking diet beverages and those drinking water.
POPULAR ARTIFICIAL SWEETENER LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DANGEROUS HEART RISK
Additionally, total cholesterol remained within the healthy range in both groups.
The findings were published in the British Journal of Nutrition.
People in both groups kept off a meaningful amount of weight for two years, even during the last year when they no longer had regular weight-management support, the researchers stated. (iStock)
"The study does not show that diet beverages themselves caused the weight loss," Alix Turoff, a registered dietitian in New York City, told Fox News Digital.
"Everyone in the study was participating in a structured weight-management program that included nutrition counseling, behavioral support and physical activity recommendations."
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Turoff, who was not involved in the study, noted that the main value of including diet beverages comes down to substitution, "not that these beverages have a magical metabolic effect."
Notably, the study compared diet beverages with water — rather than with sugar-sweetened drinks — making it a test of whether the sugar substitutes themselves appeared to hinder weight loss efforts.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"If someone normally drinks 250 calories of regular soda and switches to zero-calorie soda, then they’re saving calories," she added.
The dietitian emphasized that these findings don’t mean water and diet soda are nutritionally identical.
Both groups lost inches around their waists and hips and reduced body fat, but there was no meaningful difference between people drinking diet beverages and those drinking water. (iStock)

"The study did not find significant between-group differences in hunger or sugar intake at the end of the trial, which is relevant because one common concern is that artificial sweeteners may increase appetite or lead to compensatory eating," Turoff said.

"I would still recommend water as the primary hydration choice, but I don’t think people need to be afraid of diet drinks because they think they will automatically prevent fat loss or cause weight gain."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

There were some limitations with the research, including that it was conducted at one location in England. Race and ethnicity data were not collected, which limits the generalizability of the findings.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ

Only 220 of the 493 participants who started treatment completed the 104-week assessment. The second-year extension was also voluntary, meaning those who continued may have been more motivated or more likely to stick with the program, Turoff noted.
While the trial was funded by the American Beverage Association, the study authors stated that the association did not participate in the study design, data analysis or interpretation of the results.

title: People on weight-loss drugs report fingernails falling off as researchers uncover surprising link
summary: Nail discoloration was reported by 46% of GLP-1 users versus 17% of non-users, while scalp inflammation accompanied hair loss in most medication users studied.
story: Fox News senior medical analyst Dr. Marc Siegel analyzes study findings on 'Fox Report.'
People taking GLP-1 medications for obesity or diabetes experience nail detachment and hair loss at significantly higher rates than people with similar overall health who do not take GLP-1s.
That's according to research presented Oct. 1 at the European Academy of Dermatology and Venereology (EADV) Congress 2026 in Vienna, Austria.

Two studies evaluated 575 users of GLP-1 (glucagon-like peptide-1) drugs and a control group of 1,329 non-users, all of whom had type 2 diabetes, obesity or both. Participants were recruited across France, the U.S, Brazil and Mexico.
POPULAR WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS FACE NUMEROUS LAWSUITS OVER RARE ‘EYE STROKE’ LINKED TO VISION LOSS

In the primary study examining nail health, 39% of GLP-1 users reported nail detachment compared with 9% of non-users. Discoloration of the nails affected 46% of GLP-1 users versus 17% in the control group.
Overall, two-thirds of GLP-1 users (66%) reported experiencing at least one nail disorder, compared with 53% of the control group.

People taking GLP-1 medications for obesity or diabetes experience nail detachment and hair loss at significantly higher rates than people with similar overall health who did not take GLP-1s. (iStock)
Researchers found that weight loss alone did not explain the difference.
Even when researchers looked only at people who lost weight, those taking GLP-1s were still more likely to have these problems.
After adjusting for existing dermatological conditions and nutritional deficiencies, nail detachment and discoloration remained two to three times more frequent among the medication group.
Two-thirds (66%) of GLP-1 users experienced at least one nail issue, with nail discoloration affecting 46% of drug users compared to 17% of controls. (iStock)

"Until now, nail changes associated with GLP-1 therapies had essentially been anecdotal," study author Dr. Charles Taïeb, a clinical dermatologist at Necker University Hospital in Paris, said in a press release.
"Our findings show a clear association, but they also underline an important point: Not everything that happens during GLP-1 treatment is necessarily caused by the treatment itself."
POPULAR GLP-1 WEIGHT-LOSS DRUGS LINKED TO POTENTIALLY DEADLY BRAIN DISORDER
In another study evaluating hair and scalp conditions among the same group of participants, 50% of GLP-1 users reported unusual hair loss compared with 34% of the control group.

After starting treatment, 26% of GLP-1 users reported hair loss or thinning, compared with 12% of those not taking the drugs. Loss of hair volume was also more common, affecting 42% of GLP-1 users compared with 19% of those not taking them, the study found.
Patients taking GLP-1 receptor agonists were more than four times as likely to report nail detachment compared to non-users with similar medical profiles. (iStock)

Scalp redness was reported around three times as frequently in GLP-1 users, and hair loss among users was typically accompanied by inflammatory scalp symptoms such as itching, scaling or redness, the researchers noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"This suggests that what is happening on the scalp may go beyond the classical shedding seen after rapid weight loss and involve an inflammatory component," said study author Dr. Bruno Halioua, a Paris dermatologist, in the release.
"Scalp inflammation was the rule rather than the exception, which clinicians do not currently look for and which may be treatable."
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

Halioua stated that patients experiencing these symptoms should consult a physician rather than stopping their medication, noting that the changes are typically not serious enough to warrant discontinuing treatment.
Half of GLP-1 users reported unusual hair loss, while 42% experienced reduced hair volume or density in a study. (iStock)

The authors emphasized that because both studies relied on patient-reported data and looked at them at a single point in time, the findings only show associations and cannot prove that the medications caused these effects.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Roughly half of the GLP-1 users surveyed reported having nail issues prior to starting treatment.
The research team is planning further studies to determine when these changes occur, what may be causing them and whether they go away over time.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The studies received institutional support from DUCRAY Laboratories, a division of the Pierre Fabre Group.
Fox News Digital reached out to GLP-1 manufacturers requesting comment.

title: Shingles rates fall off a cliff among some Americans as researchers reveal likely reason
summary: Epic Research analyzed 85 million health records and found shingles rates dropped 62% among younger adults eligible for childhood chickenpox vaccination.
story: Neurologist Dr. Ajeet Sodhi breaks down research linking the shingles vaccine to a reduced risk of dementia, while stressing that the findings show an association, not proof that the vaccine treats dementia.
Shingles rates have dropped sharply among younger U.S. adults, as the first generation eligible for routine childhood chickenpox vaccination is now in their late 20s.
That’s according to a major study led by Epic Research, which analyzed the electronic health records of more than 85 million adults.
The biggest drop was between people born from 1991 to 1995 and those born from 1996 to 2000.
FDA APPROVES FIRST-EVER MRNA FLU VACCINE FOR MILLIONS OF OLDER AMERICANS

"Shingles is caused by a virus that is harbored in the peripheral nerves — varicella-zoster, the same virus that causes chickenpox — which can remain dormant and later reactivate, particularly during stress or other decreased immune responses, resulting in a shingles risk," Dr. Marc Siegel, Fox News senior medical analyst, told Fox News Digital.
Shingles rates dropped sharply among younger U.S. adults, as the first generation eligible for routine childhood chickenpox vaccination is now in their late 20s. (iStock)
About 46 out of every 10,000 people in the older group were diagnosed with shingles, compared with just 17 out of every 10,000 in the younger group — a 62% decrease.
The study period was between January 2017 and June 2026, with the findings published on Oct. 2, 2026.
CANCER VACCINE PREVENTS DEADLY MELANOMA FROM RETURNING OR SPREADING IN LANDMARK TRIAL

Overall, shingles was found to be much more common in older adults. About 182 out of every 10,000 people born between 1968 and 1975 were diagnosed with the condition, compared with just seven out of every 10,000 born between 2006 and 2008.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER

"Shingles diagnoses rise steeply with age, but the newer signal is a sharp drop that begins with people who were eligible for the childhood chickenpox vaccine in the mid-1990s," study author Kersten Bartelt, a research clinician in Verona, Wisconsin, told Fox News Digital.
"This is the pattern we would expect if childhood chickenpox vaccination lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life."
About 46 out of every 10,000 people in the older group were diagnosed with shingles, compared with just 17 out of every 10,000 in the younger group — a 62% decrease. (iStock)

If the trend continues as vaccinated groups grow older, it would suggest that childhood chickenpox vaccination could offer a lasting benefit in reducing shingles, "which is something continued follow-up and research will clarify," Bartelt added.

Siegel agreed that this data aligns with previous research showing that by preventing the initial infection via the chickenpox vaccine ("or causing a very mild version of a live virus vaccine") the risk of shingles is significantly reduced.
"This is the pattern we would expect if childhood chickenpox vaccination lowers the risk of developing shingles later in life."
He noted that the vaccine uses a weakened form of the virus, which is much less likely to reactivate later in life and cause shingles.
There were some limitations of the study, including that the researchers did not determine whether individual patients had actually received the varicella vaccination during childhood.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
"This is a descriptive, observational study, so it shows associations rather than cause and effect," Bartelt said.
Healthcare disruption due to the COVID pandemic in 2020-2021 could have also affected diagnosis rates and skewed the results, the researchers noted.

A doctor noted that while people who received the chickenpox vaccine have a lower risk of developing shingles, he still recommends that eligible people get the shingles vaccine to further reduce that risk. (iStock)
Future studies are needed to confirm a link between childhood vaccination histories and long-term shingles outcomes.

"People should continue to follow established vaccine recommendations and talk with their clinician about the shingles vaccine when they're eligible," Bartelt advised. "It's also a reminder that shingles can occur in younger adults, so anyone with a painful, blistering rash should seek timely evaluation."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
While people who received the chickenpox vaccine have a lower risk of developing shingles, Siegel said he still recommends that eligible people get the shingles vaccine to further reduce that risk.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention recommends shingles vaccination for adults 50 and older, as well as certain immunocompromised adults 19 and older, including people who previously received the varicella vaccine.

title: People who live to 100 have 3 drinks in common, longevity expert says
summary: Dan Buettner highlights how blue zones residents drink water, black coffee and red wine with resveratrol to support long-term health goals.
story: Red wine gets plenty of criticism, but it still appears in some blue zone diets. Coffee may also support healthy aging. Yet the top longevity drink is much simpler, according to longevity researcher Dan Buettner.

In the world’s "blue zones" — regions such as Sardinia, Italy, and Okinawa, Japan, known for unusually high concentrations of long-lived residents — researchers have studied dietary and lifestyle habits for clues to healthy aging and longevity.
In a recent video post, longevity researcher Dan Buettner highlighted three beverages commonly consumed in blue zones — and studies offer some clues about how each may affect health and longevity.
No. 1: Purified water
Buettner ranked water first among his three longevity drinks.
FILTERED WATER AT SPECIFIC AGES COULD ADD MONTHS TO YOUR LIFESPAN DECADES LATER, NEW STUDY FINDS

"The indisputable, best thing you can drink to live to 100 [is] water," he stated. "People in blue zones are drinking six to seven glasses of water. You want to make sure it is purified water. Water helps lower your blood pressure, helps keep your blood thin and keeps you hydrated."
Research from the National Institutes of Health indicates that proper hydration helps prevent cellular degradation, lowers the risk of chronic heart conditions and supports healthy aging. (iStock)

Research from the National Institutes of Health has linked better hydration with healthier aging, including lower risks of chronic disease and premature death, although researchers noted that the findings do not prove cause and effect.
Other health experts note that adequate water intake supports kidney function, helps regulate blood pressure and keeps blood circulating effectively.
Coffee consumption has been associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's disease. (iStock)
No. 2: Black coffee
Coffee consumption is another daily habit highlighted by Buettner, who said it is associated with lower rates of diabetes and Parkinson's.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
"Drink it black, one to two cups a day, quit by noon, it'll help you live longer," he added.
Routine coffee intake has been associated with reduced risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions. (iStock)

Coffee contains antioxidants and polyphenols, plant compounds that have been studied for their potential anti-inflammatory effects. Routine coffee consumption has also been associated with lower risks of type 2 diabetes and neurological conditions.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Limiting added sugars and heavy creams can help avoid extra calories, while consuming caffeine earlier in the day may reduce its impact on sleep.
No. 3: Red wine
Residents in blue zone areas, like Sardinia, often consume small amounts of red wine during meals.
Buettner acknowledged that red wine's place in a longevity-focused diet is "controversial."
"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the Blue Zones, and it seems to add years to life," Buettner said. (iStock)
"I'm very well aware of all the negative press wine is getting lately, but it's consumed in the blue zones and it seems to add years to life."

Red wine contains plant compounds such as resveratrol and flavonoids, which have been studied for their potential cardiovascular effects. However, experts have increasingly questioned whether any benefits attributed to red wine outweigh the known risks of alcohol.
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Alcohol consumption has been linked to numerous health risks, including an increased risk of at least seven types of cancer, according to the U.S. Surgeon General.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
People with underlying health conditions or those taking medications should consult a healthcare professional before making significant dietary changes.

title: Alan Alda reveals unexpected weapon in his battle against Parkinson's disease
summary: Alan Alda, now 90, reveals how humor and acceptance help him cope with Parkinson's disease, calling the condition "just a hobby" he lives with.
story: Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, said humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.
Alan Alda is sharing his surprising method of coping with Parkinson’s.

The actor, 90, best known for portraying Captain Benjamin Franklin "Hawkeye" Pierce in the CBS wartime sitcom "M*A*S*H," was diagnosed with the degenerative motor disease in 2015 and publicly shared the news in 2018.
The diagnosis came after the actor learned that his own behavior of acting out dreams could be an early Parkinson's symptom.
DAD JOKES MAY BE GOOD FOR YOUR BRAIN IN ONE SURPRISING WAY, EXPERTS SAY

"I had a symptom, which at the time was not that well-known: Acting out your dreams," he said in an Oct. 4 interview with CBS News. "I had a dream that somebody was attacking me. And I picked up a sack of potatoes and threw it at 'em. What I was really doing was throwing a pillow at Arlene, my wife."
Alda identified humor as his way of coping with the frustrations and limitations of the disease.
The actor, pictured with the cast of "M*A*S*H," was diagnosed with the degenerative motor disease in 2015 and publicly shared the news in 2018.  (Getty Images)

While he acknowledged the frustrations of the physical effects and limitations of Parkinson’s, he said "the best way to deal with anything that's a little bit of a problem is to find out what's funny about it and laugh at it."

In one example, he shared that when he has trouble controlling the computer mouse while composing an email, he personifies his condition as "Dr. Parkinson," moving his hand all over the screen and deleting things.
"I don't let Parkinson's define me," Alda said, joking that he sees the disease as "just a hobby."
PARKINSON’S PATIENT’S YEARS-LONG TREMOR VANISHES WITHIN MINUTES OF NEW ULTRASOUND TREATMENT
Rather than wishing he didn’t have the condition, the actor said he aims to accept his current reality.
"I really think reality is my friend," he said. "I don't want to wish it away. I can't wish it away. I can't hope for a better future. I gotta accept what is."
Arlene Alda and Alan Alda attend AARP The Magazine's 19th Annual Movies For Grownups Awards at Beverly Wilshire on Jan. 11, 2020, in Beverly Hills, California. (Getty Images)
Although Alda acknowledged that everyday tasks, such as buttoning his shirt, have become difficult, he said he treats each one like a "puzzle" to solve.

"I do hate it, but the only thing that's helpful is: What haven't I tried? And pretty soon, you get the feeling, 'If I keep looking for new ways to try this, I'll get a solution.' It's a puzzle. Will I be able eventually to put my socks on? The last time I put my socks on was a tremendous moment to celebrate!"
SCIENTISTS REVEAL SURPRISING BRAIN BENEFIT OF LAUGHTER: 'IT'S A MENTAL WORKOUT'

Dr. Chadrick Lane, a neuropsychiatrist and director of the geriatric and neuropsychiatry clinic at UT Southwestern Medical Center in Dallas, Texas, agreed that humor can be a helpful wellness tool for those navigating the Parkinson's journey.

"Humor involves cognitive reframing, this idea of looking at a circumstance through different angles — not necessarily changing the reality that one is in, but shifting the meaning and the emotional weight of the situation," an expert said. (iStock)

"Humor involves cognitive reframing, this idea of looking at a circumstance through different angles — not necessarily changing the reality that one is in, but shifting the meaning and the emotional weight of the situation," Lane, who has not treated Alda, told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
When something feels frightening or distressing, such as a medical diagnosis, creating some "psychological distance" can make a "big, big change" in perspective, he added.
Connection is another important component of humor, Lane noted.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES

"Humor is often shared. It brings us together," he said. "We are meant to share our lives with others. The importance of having a sense of belonging and humor can be a glue in that way, bringing us closer with others so that one does not go on the journey alone."
"Humor is often shared. It brings us together."
Lane shared that he has witnessed the power of humor and connection in his own practice as he cares for people living with Parkinson's disease.
"One of the wonderful things that I've seen in those settings is that, just like Mr. Alda, people crack a joke, [it] brings them a smile."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
The neuropsychiatrist also noted that Alda’s acceptance of his condition is "enormously empowering."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

"It's the idea of saying to oneself, what are the choices that I can make in the moment?" Lane told Fox News Digital. "Rarely do we ever have control over our entire day and certainly not our entire life, but we often do have control over what we choose in the moment."
"Our sense of agency is an important part of our emotional well-being."

title: New York declares measles disaster emergency as cases surge in Pennsylvania
summary: Kathy Hochul declared a statewide New York emergency as 108 measles cases spread from Pennsylvania, expanding who can administer MMR vaccines.
story: Officials are warning some travelers may have been exposed to measles at select areas inside the Philadelphia International Airport as cases rise in Pennsylvania.
New York Gov. Kathy Hochul declared a statewide emergency on Monday over a measles outbreak spreading from Pennsylvania.
It is the first time an emergency declaration has been issued since measles began surging in the U.S. in 2025.
Pennsylvania has reported 977 measles cases and five deaths as of Oct. 2, with most cases centered in rural communities. Meanwhile, New York has reported 108 cases.
WORLD’S MOST CONTAGIOUS VIRUS HITS MAJOR US AIRPORT AS OFFICIALS WARN OF POSSIBLE EXPOSURE
"No one should get seriously ill or die from a vaccine-preventable disease," Hochul said in a statement.
Kathy Hochul, governor of New York, speaks during a public safety announcement in New York on Friday, Jan. 30, 2026. (Angelina Katsanis/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
The U.S. is having its worst year for measles since 1991, with nearly 3,900 cases reported, according to the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention.
PENNSYLVANIA COMMISSIONER ACCUSES SHAPIRO OF 'DECEPTIVE' MEASLES DEATH FRAMING AS RFK JR BLASTS DEM GOVERNOR
Hochul also issued an executive order expanding the number of health professionals who are approved to administer measles vaccines.

A measles alert sign hangs outside the entrance to the Cohen Children's Medical Center, where the state health department confirmed that a baby tested positive and that there is a possibility of exposure to others at the facility, in New Hyde Park, New York, on March 14, 2025. (REUTERS/Shannon Stapleton)

The order allows registered nurses to order tests for suspected measles and pharmacists to vaccinate children as young as 2. It also requires all MMR vaccinations to be reported to state or New York City immunization registries within 72 hours, while waiving adults’ consent for such reporting.
DOCTOR SHORTAGES ARE HURTING RURAL PATIENTS. LET PHARMACISTS HELP THEM HEAL

The Pennsylvania and Philadelphia health departments, as well as the Children's Hospital of Philadelphia, reported last month that they are "working closely to ensure potentially exposed infants receive a preventative antibody product to prevent or lessen severe disease and to take steps to prevent the further spread of measles" amid the outbreak.

Sherry Andrews, right, holds 13-month-old Jaqi Herrera’s hand after administering the first MMR vaccine dose to Herrera at the City of Lubbock Health Department in Lubbock, Texas, on February 27, 2025. (Reuters)
Philadelphia Health Commissioner Dr. Palak Raval-Nelson wrote that measles exposures are "a reminder of how important it is for all of us to be up to date on our vaccinations."
MEASLES DEATHS MAY HAVE BEEN 'FABRICATED,' RFK JR CLAIMS AFTER CORONER RAISES QUESTIONS

The health department advised that anyone who has been exposed who is not immune, is unsure of their vaccination status, is an infant, is pregnant and not immune, or is immunocompromised should contact their doctor.
Girl gets checked by a doctor for measles. (iStock)

"Some people may still be eligible for treatment after exposure that can prevent measles or reduce the severity of illness," the department wrote. "Anyone who develops symptoms should call ahead before visiting a healthcare facility and tell the provider about the possible measles exposure."
MEASLES-INFECTED TRAVELER MAY HAVE EXPOSED PASSENGERS AT LAX AND NEARBY HOTEL, HEALTH OFFICIALS WARN
Measles is a highly contagious virus that can be fatal in one to three patients per 1,000 cases, data shows.

The virus can cause long-term health problems, including pneumonia and brain swelling.
Nearly 20% of individuals who contract measles are hospitalized.

title: 10 rules for living longer, seeing your grandkids grow up and enjoying your retirement savings
summary: Dr. Michael Hall shares his 10 basic longevity rules for healthy aging, from sleep and movement to purpose and social connection, in his new book.
story: Dr. Michael Hall, a Miami Beach longevity physician and author of the new book "Infinite Youth" has identified what he calls the "10 commandments of longevity," which he believes can help people extend their healthiest years.

As scientists increasingly investigate how everyday habits may influence health and aging, one longevity doctor says the keys to a longer, healthier life don't require expensive supplements, elaborate biohacks or cutting-edge treatments.

Dr. Michael Hall, a Miami Beach longevity physician and author of the new book, "Infinite Youth," has identified what he calls the "10 commandments of longevity," which he believes can help people extend their healthiest years.
Hall said the principles were shaped by nearly two decades in longevity medicine and by observing health and aging across cultures around the world.
LONGEVITY DOCTOR REVEALS WHAT MATTERS MOST FOR AGING WELL, BEYOND PRICEY BIOHACKS

"These are core elements that are not peptides, they're not NAD," Hall told Fox News Digital. "It's not that you've got to buy a fancy thing on Amazon." Instead, he said, "you start out with the basics and you maintain them consistently."
The keys to a longer, healthier life don't require expensive supplements, elaborate biohacks or cutting-edge treatments, says a longevity doctor. (iStock)
"If you’re embracing some of these things, you are doing exactly what you need to do — and these don’t cost anything."
No. 1: Guard your attention

The content that people repeatedly consume — particularly when it’s fear-based or negative — can shape their behavior, according to Hall. He sees protecting attention as part of protecting health, emphasizing the importance of being intentional about what people consume mentally.
"What you put in your mind, you need to be very careful about," he said. "What you think, you become."
ONE SIMPLE LIFESTYLE CHOICE COULD HELP YOU LIVE LONGER, SAYS LONGEVITY EXPERT
No. 2: Honor sleep
A recent study identified a "sweet spot" of about six to eight hours of sleep per day, which researchers linked to healthier aging and lower risks of premature death and disease.
Sleep is when the body recovers and the brain "resets," yet technology and poor sleep habits increasingly interfere with that process, according to Hall.

Dr. Michael Hall, a Miami Beach longevity physician and author of the new book, "Infinite Youth," has identified what he calls the "10 commandments of longevity," which he believes can help people extend their healthiest years. (Dr. Michael Hall)
"Sleep is probably one of the most important things that we just don’t talk about enough," he said.
The expert pointed out that the body’s circadian rhythm responds naturally to light and darkness, while screens, artificial light and late bedtimes can disrupt that cycle.
"The bed is really for sleep and sex," Hall added.
No. 3: Move daily
A September 2026 study found that highly active older adults maintained high levels of aerobic fitness into their 60s, 70s and 80s, despite some normal age-related decline.
"Movement is life," Hall agreed. He recalled seeing older adults remain highly active during his time working in New Zealand and Sri Lanka, including women in their 90s who were still mobile and fit.
3 COMMON FACTORS MAY BE SECRETLY SPEEDING UP THE AGING PROCESS, EXPERT SAYS
Hall’s own routine includes walking, swimming, cycling and resistance work.
For everyday movement, he particularly recommends walking and squatting, which engage large muscle groups and help maintain strength and mobility.
No. 4: Preserve strength
Muscle strength helps support bones, posture and mobility, and may help reduce frailty and fall risk later in life, according to the longevity expert.
"You need to maintain that good, healthy posture and strength throughout your life," Hall said.
Muscle strength helps support bones, posture and mobility and may help reduce frailty and fall risk later in life. (iStock)
He connected loss of movement and strength with weakening muscles, bones, tendons and ligaments, potentially increasing fall risk as people age.
"If you’re moving, you’re preserving strength, you’re maintaining your bones, because they go together," Hall said.
No. 5: Eat real food
For optimal longevity nutrition, Hall recommends choosing minimally processed foods, with a focus on simple preparation, portion control and awareness of what goes into meals.
"Food is medicine, food is fuel, food is life," Hall said.
CLICK HERE TO SIGN UP FOR OUR HEALTH NEWSLETTER
While Hall said he cooks his own meals, primarily chooses fresh foods and largely avoids foods that come "out of a bag or a box," he emphasizes portion control rather than complete deprivation.
"I don’t care what it is you love, you can have a bite," he said.
No. 6: Embrace purpose
Having a mission gives people something beyond themselves to invest in, contributing to emotional well-being and a meaningful life, according to Hall.
"It’s the most important part of being human," he said. "Our mission … is our purpose."
Hall recommends choosing minimally processed foods, with a focus on simple preparation, portion control and awareness of what goes into meals. (iStock)

That purpose does not have to come from an extraordinary calling, Hall suggested. Whether someone is a physician, firefighter, baker or coffee shop owner, serving others can provide a sense of meaning.
"If you’re just serving yourself, you aren’t going to be a happy person," he added.
No. 7: Cultivate meaningful relationships
"No one ages well alone," Hall said. "You cannot live alone. You’re not designed to be atomized living in a box alone."
Research published in October 2026 in PLOS One found that loneliness was associated with a higher risk of death at one, three and five years.
CLICK HERE FOR MORE HEALTH STORIES
Hall also pointed to companionship, family and meaningful relationships as important parts of his own life.
"Having people around you who appreciate you, who you can relate to, who can have a conversation with, have a laugh with, it’s so important," he said.
No. 8: Welcome challenge
A 2025 study of more than 10,000 older adults with cognitive impairment found that greater participation in cognitively stimulating activities was associated with a lower risk of death over time.
"We’re needing to be challenged … as an individual and as a community and as society," Hall said.
No. 9: Remain curious
Continuing to learn, explore and seek out new experiences could play a role in healthy aging, research has found.
"No one ages well alone," the expert said. "You cannot live alone. You’re not designed to be atomized living in a box alone." (iStock)
Hall similarly believes curiosity helps people remain engaged with the world as they get older.
"Curiosity allows us to explore and to always be aware there’s something more," he told Fox News Digital. "You’re never going to know everything. So you’re always on the quest."
TEST YOURSELF WITH OUR LATEST LIFESTYLE QUIZ
Curiosity has driven much of Hall’s travel and work around the world, he said, noting that getting older shouldn't mean stopping the pursuit of new experiences.
"We were children, and we never really grew up, by the way — we just get older in our bodies."
No. 10: Keep the funnel wide
In his book, Hall describes healthy aging as keeping the body's metaphorical "funnel" as wide as possible for as long as possible.
He sees aging as a gradual narrowing of that funnel, with increasing physiological stress as the body loses some of its ability to maintain optimal function.
"We were children, and we never really grew up — we just get older in our bodies."
Keeping the funnel wide, he said, means supporting overall health and resilience through the fundamental habits outlined in his other commandments.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Ultimately, Hall said his goal is not simply to help people accumulate more birthdays, but to make those additional years healthier and more meaningful.
"I’m selling healthspan as much as I possibly can," he said. "Your best years of your life, the best living you can possibly have, sharing with others and making society better."
Melissa Rudy is senior health editor and a member of the lifestyle team at Fox News Digital. Story tips can be sent to melissa.rudy@fox.com.

title: Republican lawmakers break with Trump on diesel deal with Russia
summary: Some Republican lawmakers voiced staunch opposition after United States President Donald Trump announced a diesel agreement with Russia.
story: Crude oil prices climb as lawmakers press President Donald Trump Trump to abandon his controversial Russia diesel deal. Former U.S. Energy Secretary Dan Brouillette breaks down the global energy market, analyzing the economic fallout of the potential agreement on domestic supply.

President Donald Trump last week touted a diesel agreement with Russian President Vladimir Putin, asserting that prices for the fuel would swiftly fall, but some Republicans have responded by rebuking the president's move.

"I have just concluded a highly successful discussion with President Vladimir Putin, of Russia, wherein it was agreed that Russia will immediately supply over 300,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel to the American and Global Marketplace, another 500,000 Tons during the month of November, and 1,000,000 Tons immediately thereafter. Additionally, based on the condition of their Diesel Refineries, Russia will then deliver, within a short period of time, 3,000,000 Tons of Diesel Fuel," Trump declared in an Oct. 9 Truth Social post.

"Between our TOTAL CONTROL of the Strait of Hormuz, and this great announcement on Russian Energy, Diesel Prices for Americans and, indeed, the World, will be COMING DOWN, IN RECORD NUMBERS, AND FAST! Lower prices for Americans, especially our Great Farmers, Ranchers, and Truckers, is my Greatest Priority. This is a very big and important announcement. Additionally, it must be understood, that Iran will not have a Nuclear Weapon!" Trump declared.
The announcement sparked blowback from some Republicans, including outgoing Rep. Don Bacon of Nebraska, who declared in a post on X that Trump's "policies towards Russia and Ukraine are failures."
ZELENSKYY ACCUSES PUTIN OF DEFYING TRUMP'S CEASEFIRE PUSH, SENDS POINTED MESSAGE TO WHITE HOUSE
U.S. President Donald Trump (R) greets Russian President Vladimir Putin as he arrives at Joint Base Elmendorf-Richardson on Aug. 15, 2025 in Anchorage, Alaska. (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
"Propping up Putin’s war economy is morally wrong as he uses that money to bomb cities," Bacon asserted. "We need moral clarity not moral ambiguity."

Rep. Brian Fitzpatrick, R-Pa., declared in a post on Saturday, "We will be introducing bipartisan legislation to block any and all purchases of Russian oil. It will be called the 'Ronald Reagan Peace Through Strength Act.' It will be forced to the Floor via discharge and it will pass overwhelmingly."
Bacon shared Fitzpatrick's post and noted, "I’ve already agreed to be an original cosponsor. Congress must make a stand."

A bipartisan group of senators — including Democratic Sens. Jeanne Shaheen of New Hampshire, Richard Blumenthal of Connecticut, Ron Wyden of Oregon, as well as GOP Sens. Susan Collins of Maine, Lisa Murkowski of Alaska, Thom Tillis of North Carolina and John Curtis of Utah — joined together in a statement pressing the administration to "reverse course."

"Congress explicitly banned Russian energy imports in 2022 to prevent American dollars from financing Putin’s brutal war against Ukraine. Congress was clear: The U.S. should not import oil from Russia until it ends its aggression against Ukraine and ceases threats against our NATO Allies," the statement declares.
TRUMP RUSSIA DEAL COULD FUEL PUTIN'S WAR, EX-NATO COMMANDER WARNS AS ZELENSKYY SAYS 'NYET'
Rep. Don Bacon, R-Neb., arrives at a House Republican Conference meeting in the U.S. Capitol Building on July 21, 2026, in Washington, D.C. (Anna Moneymaker/Getty Images)

"President Trump’s decision to allow Russian diesel imports to the U.S. runs directly counter to that law. The Administration has also failed to consult with Congress or submit any explanation to justify its decision as required by statute. The United States should not provide Putin with a financial lifeline while Russia continues to kill Ukrainian civilians. The Administration must immediately reverse course," the statement adds.
Tillis, an outgoing senator who is not seeking re-election, is the author of the recently released book, "How to Lose Friends and Antagonize Presidents." Shaheen is also not seeking another term.
Former U.S. Energy Secretary Dan Brouillette explained during a Monday appearance on FOX Business that he does not expect the agreement to cause the price of diesel to decline significantly.

He said that he believes "it's important for Americans to realize that ... we may not be talking about brand new barrels to the marketplace. So if there's an expectation that prices are gonna come down dramatically as a result of this agreement, I'm a bit skeptical of that."
TRUMP CALLS FOR UKRAINE TO REPLACE ZELENSKYY AFTER CLASH OVER RUSSIA DIESEL DEAL: 'GET A NEW PRESIDENT'
Sen. Thom Tillis, R-N.C., during a Bloomberg Television interview in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Oct. 7, 2026. (Stefani Reynolds/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Brouillette said that if the aim is to decrease "prices in the long term," then it is "challenging to see how this is going to help. What we're in essence doing is rearranging the barrels," Brouillette explained, "we're moving the barrels from one customer to another customer. We're not producing new barrels of diesel, which is really what the market is expecting and wanting."
Fox News Digital reached out to the White House on Monday.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: US attorney warns Chinese espionage is 'extremely pervasive,' says Beijing 'playing the long game'
summary: First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli says Chinese espionage is "extremely pervasive" after his office charged alleged spies in recent months.
story: First Assistant US Attorney Bill Essayli told Fox News Digital that Chinese government-backed espionage is "extremely pervasive" in the U.S.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli said Chinese espionage is "extremely pervasive" in the U.S. following the arrest of an alleged Chinese agent in Los Angeles this month.

Essayli told Fox News Digital in an interview that his office has pressed charges against several alleged Chinese spies in recent months, saying Beijing is brazen in its attempts to build their access inside the U.S.

"I think it's extremely pervasive," Essayli said of Chinese spying. "China is one of our biggest adversaries, and they're committed to advancing their interests. And they're playing the long game, and so they are willing to put a lot of resources into developing sources, recruiting people within the U.S. to advance their interests.
CHINA EXPERT WARNS BEIJING WANTS AMERICANS — NOT THE CCP — TO SPREAD ITS MESSAGE

First Assistant United States Attorney for the Central District of California Bill Essayli speaks as U.S. and Canadian law enforcement officials announce federal charges and arrests of alleged members of a transnational organized crime group at FBI offices in Los Angeles, Calif., on July 7, 2026. (REUTERS)

"They're willing to steal our technology; they're willing to engage in espionage here. So, there's no limit to what China is willing to do. It is a huge, huge concern. We have to be vigilant, and we have to disrupt these operations on our soil," Essayli said. "We have to protect our sovereignty."

"If you look at just the cases we brought this year, just in my office, I mean, you had cases where the woman from Irvine was engaged in espionage against the Taiwanese president's family member. I had a guy last week we arrested, he sold more than $300 million in SI chips, formerly known as AI chips, to China," he continued. "You had a mayor of a local city that we charged for serving as an unregistered agent of China as well, pushing out their propaganda and taking orders from China."
FORMER CALIFORNIA MAYOR ADMITS TO SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING BEIJING PROPAGANDA IN US
This photo provided by the Federal Bureau of Investigation shows Wanying Zhang being arrested Sunday, Oct. 4, 2026, in Los Angeles. (Federal Bureau of Investigation via AP)

"So, it's extremely pervasive. It's a huge problem, but the FBI is on it," he said. "They have entire squads dedicated to combating this, and we're committed here at the U.S. Attorney's Office to supporting those investigations and bringing criminal charges to disrupt these operations."

Wanying Zhang, 34, of Irvine, was arrested earlier this month for allegedly working with an associate to photograph and record the family outside their Seattle-area home, according to a criminal complaint obtained by Fox News Digital.
CHINA-LINKED HACKERS INFILTRATED US GOVERNMENT NETWORKS BEFORE FBI TAKEDOWN
Authorities nabbed Zhang, who goes by "Heather" in the U.S., at the Los Angeles airport as she attempted to board a plane to China.
This undated photo released by the U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California on Monday, Oct. 5, 2026, shows Wanying Zhang. (U.S. Attorney for the Central District of California via AP)
Essayli said FBI Los Angeles agents arrested Zhang on a federal charge of acting as an unregistered agent of the People’s Republic of China.
CALIFORNIA MAYOR ACCUSED OF SECRETLY WORKING FOR CHINA, SPREADING PROPAGANDA WHILE IN OFFICE: FEDS
She allegedly traveled to Seattle in 2025 at the direction of Chinese officials and sent them photos, videos and license plate information.

"She coordinated the trip with an associate and used tradecraft to avoid detection," Essayli wrote. "She never notified the attorney general she was acting for a foreign government, a federal offense."
GOOGLE ENGINEER STOLE AI SECRETS FOR CHINA, SENATE HEARS IN EXPLOSIVE TESTIMONY
Former Arcadia Mayor Eileen Wang exits federal court after pleading guilty to acting as an illegal foreign agent on behalf of the Chinese government. (William Liang/Associated Press)
Speaking on "The Big Weekend Show" Sunday, Essayli said Zhang is a naturalized U.S. citizen and confirmed the alleged surveillance targeted a relative of Taiwan’s president.
"She was conducting surveillance on behalf of the Chinese government. She was acting as a foreign agent," Essayli said. "And she was spying on a relative of the president of Taiwan here in the U.S."
The alleged target was Ting-Yu Lai, the U.S.-based son of Taiwanese President Lai Ching-te, CBS News reported, citing law enforcement sources. The complaint does not name him.
First Assistant U.S. Attorney Bill Essayli speaks at a Los Angeles press conference announcing developments in a terrorism investigation on Dec. 15, 2025. (Damian Dovarganes/AP)
"Saw him. Young male. It’s that young one," Zhang allegedly messaged a Chinese government contact while outside the home.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
"I am video recording," she allegedly added before sending two license plate numbers.
Anders Hagstrom is a reporter with Fox News Digital covering national politics and major breaking news events.

title: Democrats see new chances to flip red states — but a $400M GOP spending advantage could derail their plans
summary: Republicans outspend Democrats by $400 million ahead of Election Day, forcing Senate Majority PAC to make tough choices across nine battlegrounds.
story: Democrat-aligned Senate Majority PAC Communications Director Lauren French, in a Fox News Digital interview, sounds alarm over GOP spending advantage as Senate battleground map expands

With just over three weeks to go until Election Day, more and more red states and congressional districts appear in reach for the Democrats, as they work to win back House and Senate majorities from the Republicans in the midterms. But a massive Republican spending advantage threatens to complicate those ambitions.

Republican campaigns, committees and aligned groups have outspent their Democratic counterparts by $400 million so far this election cycle, according to AdImpact, a leading political advertising tracking firm.
The disparity is forcing Democrats to make difficult decisions about where to invest and how much to spend as the party tries to expand the electoral map.

"We are being outspent by the Republicans. That's just a fact," Lauren French, communications director at the Senate Majority PAC, told Fox News Digital. "In many of these states, they have really transactionalized elections, so they have monopoly money to play with, whereas we are working with real resources."
DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS FORMER - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT
Fox News Power Rankings on Senate forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)

The latest Fox News Power Rankings shifted GOP-dominated South Carolina from Solid to Likely Republican. The Senate showdown in reliably Republican Kansas is Lean Republican, while the races in red-leaning Alaska, Iowa, Ohio and Texas are rated toss-ups.
"Senate Majority PAC has resources to compete, and we are very happy that we're able to be in 9 battleground states," French said.
The super PAC is the leading outside group supporting Democratic Senate candidates and incumbents and is aligned with longtime Democratic leader Sen. Chuck Schumer.
French highlighted record-setting fundraising over the past three months, but added, "of course, more recess resources would be helpful."
With the latest polls from Fox News and other organizations showing Democrats increasingly competitive across the Senate map, the party is pleading for more money.

"Last month a pro-Trump PAC reserved $10 million in New Hampshire advertising, and we’re being outspent 3-to-1," reads a fundraising pitch to supporters by Rep. Chris Pappas, the Democratic Senate nominee in swing state New Hampshire.
WHO'S UP AND WHO'S DOWN IN THE LATEST FOX NEWS MIDTERM POWER RANKINGS
Rep. Chris Pappas of New Hampshire, the Democratic Senate nominee, speaks at a state party event on Oct. 3, 2026 in Concord, N.H. (Paul Steinhauser/Fox News)

Senate Majority PAC is rushing some of its record fundraising into the newly competitive battlegrounds. And American Bridge PAC, a Democrat-aligned group, recently pumped over $20 million into South Carolina and Kansas, as well as competitive races in two other red states, Florida and Mississippi.

But the Democratic groups are being outspent by their Republican-aligned counterparts, thanks to major expenditures by Senate Leadership Fund, the President Donald Trump-allied MAGA Inc. and a super PAC bankrolled by Elon Musk.

"The hard reality is there isn't enough funding to protect the toss-up states and also heavily invest in the red-leaning states where we're playing offense," a veteran Democratic Senate operative who requested anonymity to speak candidly told Fox News Digital."

French told Fox News Digital "This is the time in the campaign season where everyone really has to make some of those belt-tightening decisions, and that's why we're looking at every race really closely to make sure we have enough resources to get to the majority, but we're also not leaving anyone shortchanged."
House Democrats are facing a similar predicament.

A memo from the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee (DCCC) shared with donors warned that Republicans "are now flooding districts across our battlefield with MAGA Inc. and Trump super PAC money that we simply cannot match."
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB
Fox News Power Rankings forecast for the House of Representatives. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
The memo, which was obtained by Fox News Digital, requested an additional $17 million that was needed by Oct. 22 "to close the sale" in what they described as "winnable races."

The GOP is fighting political history, which has traditionally seen the party in power in Washington lose congressional seats during midterm election years. Add to that a challenging political climate fueled by persistent inflation Americans see at the grocery store, high gas prices tied to what polls show is an unpopular war with Iran and Trump's negative approval ratings.
SIGN UP TO GET THE POLITICS NEWSLETTER
But the Republicans' financial advantage has allowed GOP campaigns and allied groups to spend more on political advertising nationally.

"Thanks to the tireless efforts of Leader John Thune, Senate Leadership Fund has amassed a financial advantage that neither party has had before. SLF will continue to invest unprecedented resources across the map to maintain the Republican Senate majority," Senate Leadership Fund communications director Chris Gustafson told Fox News Digital.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

Veteran GOP strategist Jesse Hunt told Fox News Digital that "Republican outside groups will have played a decisive role in positive Republican performance if they have a good election night despite what is strong headwinds working against them."
"This is not an advantage Republicans typically have and it's definitely a contributing factor to a lot of candidates on the ballot right now keeping their races close," Hunt emphasized.
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: SC Dem Senate candidate claims she will stand up to her party as Graham ties her to 'socialist Democrats'
summary: Democratic South Carolina U.S. Senate candidate Annie Andrews and Republican Sen. Darline Graham clashed during a U.S. Senate election debate.
story: Republican Sen. Darline Graham and Democratic opponent Annie Andrews clashed during the South Carolina U.S. Senate election debate on October 11, 2026. (Courtesy: SCETV)
Sen. Darline Graham, R-S.C., and Democratic challenger Annie Andrews clashed on Sunday night during the South Carolina U.S. Senate debate, which also included Libertarian candidate Kasie Whitener.

Graham said she is "concerned about the socialist Democrats," asserting that after Hamas terrorists slaughtered Israelis on Oct. 7, 2023, Democrats in New York cheered "over the death of over a thousand people."
"Annie Andrews will not stand up to the socialist Democratic Party. She's only going to join them," Graham declared.
DARLINE GRAHAM'S 'EMBARRASSING AND INEXCUSABLE' NATIONAL SECURITY STUMBLE SPOTLIGHTS BREAK FROM LATE BROTHER

Senator Darline Graham, R-S.C., speaks to members of the media after casting her ballot at a polling location inside Lake Murray Baptist Church during a special primary election in Lexington, S.C., on Tuesday, Aug. 11, 2026. (Sam Wolfe/Bloomberg via Getty Images)
Andrews fired back, claiming that she is willing to stand up to her party.

"I told you my opponent was going to call me a socialist and there she's done it again. She's been told to come out here and call me Bernie, Ocasio, Mamdani. That's what's in her script," Andrews said, referring to Sen. Bernie Sanders, I-Vt., Rep. Alexandria Ocasio-Cortez, D-N.Y., and New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani.
"But the truth is my name is Annie Andrews. And there shouldn't be any confusion about that because unlike my opponent, I haven't changed my name recently," she said.
DEMOCRATS ARE CHANGING THEIR TRANSGENDER MESSAGE. REPUBLICANS SAY THEY'RE JUST FLIP-FLOPPING
South Carolina Democratic Senate candidate Dr. Annie Andrews speaks during a campaign stop at the Columbia Bethlehem Community Center on Oct. 6, 2026 in Columbia, S.C. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

"The real difference between me and Sen. Graham is that I will stand up to my own party and I will always put South Carolina first. She seems to believe the job she has right now is to be the White House's ambassador to South Carolina. The job is to represent South Carolina. She considers the job to be to read their scripts and do their bidding. And we can do better," Andrews asserted.

Graham fired back, saying that her "legal name is Graham" and "has always been Graham." She explained, "I lost my parents when I was a little girl, and I kept the name Graham so that I felt connected to them. So my name, every document I have ever signed, has Graham on it."
After the death of Sen. Lindsey Graham, South Carolina Gov. Henry McMaster tapped the late lawmaker's sister Darline to serve the remainder of her brother's Senate term.

title: Drag queens, trans pastor, abortion rallies: Inside Dem governor hopeful's progressive church
summary: Rob Sand regularly attended Plymouth Congregational United Church of Christ, which has hosted drag queen concerts and invited a transgender pastor.
story: Iowa Democrats Rob Sand and Josh Turek flatly reject campaign support from Kamala Harris as they campaign for governor and Senate.

In one of the most hotly contested governor's races in the country, the Democratic nominee has been working overtime to cultivate a moderate image — while reportedly attending a church that openly embraces some of the progressive causes dividing voters in Iowa.

Rob Sand, Iowa’s state auditor and its Democratic nominee for governor, regularly attended Plymouth Congregational United Church of Christ, located in the state’s capital, as of late 2025, according to a local journalist. Over the years, Plymouth has hosted and promoted drag queen performances, invited a transgender pastor to serve as a guest pastor and openly supported abortion.

Sand has emphasized his faith on the campaign trail, repeatedly referencing Christianity and quoting scripture, at times successfully appealing to otherwise conservative Iowans. In addition to leaning on his faith, Sand has repeatedly described himself as independently minded, claimed to have voted for Republicans in the past and said that he sometimes prefers working with the GOP over Democrats, calling political parties "poison."

"I am a Christian. I’m a conservative. But I’m not a party-based person," one voter is quoted as saying in a Sand press release. "I like to vote for the person as opposed to the party. And to me, (Sand) just seems really honest and down to earth. And I enjoyed him."
IOWA GUBERNATORIAL HOPEFUL ZACH LAHN TELLS 'RUTHLESS' DEMOCRATS ARE HIDING THEIR BAD POLICIES
Gubernatorial candidate Rob Sand speaks to voters during a campaign visit to the Carroll County Conservation Classroom on Aug. 20, 2026, in Carroll, Iowa. (Leon Neal/Getty Images)

Sand's reported church attendance, however, connects him to a congregation whose progressive religious and political positions stand in contrast to the moderate image he has emphasized on the campaign trail.

Sand’s church is open about its progressive slant, with its "about" page featuring an image of churchgoers at a gay pride parade, noting that the church does not take the Bible literally and stating that it "has been an LGBTQ+ Open and Affirming congregation for more than 30 years."
An image of the church included in a profile compiled by the United Church of Christ shows it flying a pride flag on its grounds, noting that the church "is a progressive powerhouse in the region."

"Rob Sand goes to church weekly and does so in Iowa, unlike Zach Lahn. Rob’s faith is deeply important to him, and like many, he has never found a church where he agrees with everything, but does prefer traditional services with liturgy and classic hymns," a spokeswoman for his campaign told Fox News Digital. "Rob has always been independent-minded, and he isn’t going to take lessons in morality from a sex toy salesman who lives in Kansas."

The mention of sex toys was a reference to FirmTech, a company that manufactures wearable sexual wellness devices and once counted GOP gubernatorial nominee Zach Lahn as an investor. Lahn maintains that the product was originally developed to monitor cardiovascular health and that he divested before the company shifted toward more sexually suggestive marketing.

Sand has also pointed to Lahn's regular flights to Kansas, arguing that they betray tenuous ties to the state he's seeking to govern. Lahn, meanwhile, says that he lives full-time in Iowa, explaining that the flights are a product of him needing to shuttle children from a previous marriage between the two states.
Lahn's campaign did not divulge where he attends church when asked by Fox News Digital.
LGBTQ GROUP REVEALS WHICH DEM NOMINEE IS SPONSORING HALLOWEEN EVENT FEATURING DRAG SHOWS

The Iowa State Capitol building is seen on October 9, 2019, in Des Moines, Iowa. The 2020 Iowa Democratic caucuses will take place on February 3, 2020, making it the first nominating contest in the Democratic Party presidential primaries. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)
Plymouth’s progressive reputation is well-earned.

In May 2025, Plymouth hosted drag queen "Flamy Grant" for a concert, according to advertisements for the event, bringing an artist whose broader catalog includes sexually explicit lyrics to the progressive Des Moines congregation.

In one song, titled "Take a Chance on Me," not to be confused with the ABBA classic of the same name, Grant sings, "I’m a patient lover unless I finish first. And I expect you [to] finish me if the roles are reversed. I maintain the mystery of my sexual history."

In another song, the drag queen complained about his childhood church, stating that "I guess the lesson there was God would only hear a prayer If it came from a person with a c---." The song continues to state that "secretly most men just fear the snatch" and praises Eve for disobeying God by eating the forbidden fruit.
POWERFUL LGBTQ+ GROUP'S ENDORSEMENTS COULD TANK VULNERABLE DEMS OVER RADICAL YOUTH TRANS AGENDA
Democratic Party candidate for Iowa governor, Rob Sand. (Rob Sand For Iowa)

About a year later, Plymouth promoted a drag event on its Facebook page at a nearby church billed as a "family-friendly karaoke fundraiser" headlined by drag queen "Tess Tura." Tura hosts a podcast where, among other topics, unprotected gay sex is discussed.

In a similar vein, Plymouth invited transgender pastor Paula Stone Williams to serve as a guest pastor for one weekend in 2023, according to a local media report. At the time, Williams had recently published a book titled "As a Woman: What I learned about power, sex, and the patriarchy after I transitioned."
VULNERABLE DEM'S CAMPAIGN PITCH CLASHES WITH 'RADICAL' VOTING RECORD ON TOP CULTURE WAR ISSUE
The Des Moines skyline is seen from the lookout at Two Rivers Park on Oct. 9, 2025, in Des Moines, Iowa. (Cody Scanlan/The Register / USA TODAY NETWORK via Imagn Images)
Some of Plymouth’s pro-LGBTQ advocacy is directed at young children.

Plymouth disclosed in a 2025 job posting that it partners with the Rainbow Faith Coalition, a group that says "LGBTQ+ identities are God-given, honored and celebrated," and that "[f]ully living into these identities in name, pronoun, relationship and gender expression is not a barrier to participation … in any areas of the faith community," including children’s programming and education.

The church also offers Our Whole Lives programming, a sexuality education curriculum co-published by the Unitarian Universalist Association and the United Church of Christ, with classes beginning in first grade that address topics including sexuality, relationships, gender identity and sexual health.
Similar to its theology, the church’s politics are decidedly liberal.
TOP CONSERVATIVE GROUP UNVEILS FULL-COURT PRESS IN KEY BATTLEGROUND STATE TO EXPOSE ‘SHOCKING’ DEM PLATFORM
Iowa Republican nominee for governor Zach Lahn speaks to fairgoers at the Iowa State Fair on Aug. 14, 2026, in Des Moines, Iowa. (Scott Olson/Getty Images)

In February 2025, for example, Plymouth’s pastors joined a protest in Iowa’s statehouse "to pray and stand up for our trans and gender nonconforming friends and neighbors," per a post on the church's Facebook page. A few years prior, church leadership participated in a pro-LGBTQ rally outside the statehouse, according to another church Facebook post.

"Plymouth’s bold social justice presence is a hallmark in the community and is often cited as a reason for new members joining the congregation," a church job posting from 2025 reads. "We are committed to advancing justice, equity, and compassion in and beyond our community."

Indeed, as the Supreme Court struck down Roe v. Wade, Plymouth mobilized to fight against pro-life legislation, supporting those fighting for "reproductive healthcare" and referring to women as "all who hold the potential to bear life." The church held a prayer vigil in support of abortion in May 2022 and rallied at the state capital in July 2023 to protest against efforts to regulate abortion.

After former President Joe Biden became the first president to formally recognize Transgender Day of Visibility in 2021, Plymouth followed his lead by sending Facebook messages to its followers observing Transgender Day of Visibility and Transgender Day of Remembrance between 2021 and 2023.
