"This is disturbing material, but it’s right in line with Rob Sand’s liberal views. If you believe men can become women, then what’s to stop you from teaching it to schoolchildren?" a spokesperson for the Lahn campaign told Fox News Digital. "Values matter and Rob’s values are NOT Iowa values."

title: Federal agents raid Ilhan Omar’s DC home amid immigration fraud investigation
summary: Rep. Ilhan Omar's home was the subject of a pre-dawn HSI raid.
story: Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital.
EXCLUSIVE: The home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn, was raided early Monday morning by Homeland Security Investigations (HSI), a source familiar with the matter told Fox News Digital.
Multiple federal agents with HSI jackets were seen outside Omar's Washington, D.C. home in the early hours of Monday.

Two sources close to the investigation say the search stems from a criminal fraud investigation into the Somali-born congresswoman's immigration paperwork, which was filled out by her late father when she was a child.
Omar responded to the raid on X, slamming it as a way for President Donald Trump to "target political enemies" with "baseless lies," and insisted: "I will not be silenced."

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C., home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., early Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital.   (Andrew Murray/Fox News Digital)
OMAR'S GOP CHALLENGER COMES OUT FIRING WITH VOW TO CLEAN UP 'MESS' IN DEEP BLUE DISTRICT: 'PEOPLE ARE FED UP'

The raid of the Somali-born congresswoman's home started around 6 a.m. with HSI and Department of Homeland Security (DHS) leading the operation. The Department of Justice (DOJ) is also involved in the investigation.

"Today in the Washington, D.C., area, Homeland Security Investigations executed a judicially authorized search warrant secured by the Department of Justice. This enforcement action is part of an ongoing federal investigation," a DOJ spokesperson told Fox News Digital.
The DOJ later added that the investigation was "criminal" in nature.
A spokesperson for Omar did not respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. The White House and DHS spokespeople declined to provide comment.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC.  (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)

Federal agents with Homeland Security Investigations (HSI) raided the Washington, D.C. home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on Monday morning, a source familiar with the operation told Fox News Digital. (Fox News Digital/Andrew Murray)
"I’m ok," Omar wrote on X hours after the search commenced. "Make no mistake: this is an attempt to target political enemies and weaponize federal law enforcement."
"For ten years, Trump has targeted me with baseless lies and smear campaigns," she continued. "This is just the latest escalation in his campaign of political intimidation. I will not be silenced."

President Donald Trump's Border Czar Tom Homan said in mid-September that the progressive congresswoman was subject to an ongoing "criminal" investigation, but did not specify the nature of the probe.
Homeland Security Investigations police search the home of Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., on October 12, 2026 in Washington, DC.  (Andrew Leyden/Getty Images)
WATCH: OMAR SILENT WHEN CONFRONTED ON ALLEGED TIES TO MASSIVE MINNESOTA FRAUD SCANDAL

HSI is the principal investigative arm of DHS. Its scope includes investigating cross-border crime and global threats, including human trafficking and child sexual exploitation, drug smuggling and cybercrime. HSI plays a major front-line role in America’s counterterrorism operations.
Omar has been under fire for months and faced a myriad of controversies during her time in Congress. Most recently, her financial disclosures have come into focus.
In 2024, the congresswoman reported that her husband possessed between $6 million and $30 million in assets.

A more recent 2025 financial disclosure report shows Omar’s revised value of shared assets between her and husband to sit at a maximum of $125,000 — a multimillion-dollar drop from the year prior, a difference of about 29.9 million. The lower estimate of their assets, $20,000, compared to the low and high debt estimates, $30,000 and $100,000, would imply the Minnesota Democrat could have a negative net worth.
Rep. Ilhan Omar calls out President Trump and Elon Musk for handling of USAID while also accusing the president of running a dictatorship. (Pool)
ILHAN OMAR'S OFFICE SAYS SHE'S ‘NOT A MILLIONAIRE’ AFTER $30M FILING REVISED DOWN TO UNDER $100K: REPORT
Both she and her husband have separate debts, each ranging somewhere between $15,000 and $50,000 — from her own student loans and her husband’s credit card debt, according to the disclosures.
Omar has repeatedly refused to clarify the disclosures.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
During her tenure in Congress, she has been plagued by allegations that she married her brother in 2009 in an alleged immigration fraud scheme.
A federal prosecutor recently told Fox News Digital that the statute of limitations could hinder an investigation into that matter.
Additionally, Omar made headlines this summer after her son's residence was raided in connection to allegations his felon roommate possessed illegal firearms and ammunition.
Fox News' Hannah Brennan contributed to this report.
Peter D'Abrosca is a politics reporter at Fox News Digital.

title: Trump's backyard is quietly transforming into 'Silicon Valley South' as wealthy Americans flock in
summary: Palm Beach is drawing tech giants and Wall Street executives, says real estate expert Margit Brandt, who compares the region to Silicon Valley.
story: Florida-based real estate agent, Margit Brandt, told Fox News Digital that millionaires are seeking better quality of life in Florida.

A wealthy Southern enclave once known as a playground for retirees and snowbirds is transforming into a growing technology and financial hub, drawing comparisons to Silicon Valley as businesses, Wall Street executives and entrepreneurs move in.
Palm Beach County, Florida, is attracting new attention as wealthy Americans seek alternatives to high-tax states like New York and California.

"Palm Beach has changed from a place where people come to retire to a place that people come to build," luxury real estate expert Margit Brandt told Fox News Digital. "There's been countless CEOs and major heads of companies that have moved their businesses to Palm Beach," she said, pointing to Florida's favorable tax climate and lifestyle as major draws.
THE RED STATES RACING AHEAD IN AMERICA’S POWERFUL WEALTH BOOM — AND THE STATES FALLING BEHIND

Long known as a playground for the rich and famous, Palm Beach, Florida, is emerging as a growing business and technology hub, attracting wealthy executives, entrepreneurs and major companies. (Saul Martinez/Bloomberg/Getty Images)

The region is also home to President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate, often dubbed the "Southern White House," placing the emerging business hub in the backyard of one of the country's most recognizable political landmarks.

The shift comes amid changing migration patterns across the country, with Internal Revenue Service data for 2022–2023 showing taxpayer losses across numerous California and Northeastern counties, while much of the Southeast recorded gains.
Brandt believes Palm Beach County could become a major technology hub, citing its room for expansion as an advantage over more densely developed destinations.

"We have tons of room to grow," she said, pointing to areas like Wellington and western Palm Beach County where new schools, hospitals and infrastructure could accommodate additional businesses and families.
The region is also attracting technology investment alongside its established financial services industry.
In September 2025, California-based software company ServiceNow announced plans to establish a regional innovation hub and artificial intelligence institute in West Palm Beach.
AMERICANS KEEP MOVING TO TEXAS AND FLORIDA — BUT ONE OTHER RED STATE IS GROWING EVEN FASTER

President Donald Trump's Mar-a-Lago estate in Palm Beach, Florida, sits at the heart of a wealthy enclave increasingly attracting technology companies, Wall Street executives and entrepreneurs. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The expansion is projected to generate $1.8 billion in economic impact and create more than 850 jobs over five years, according to the company. ServiceNow also committed to occupying up to 200,000 square feet of office space at 10 CityPlace, a development by billionaire real estate investor Stephen Ross's Related Ross.
"The tech has particularly been exciting for Palm Beach County," Brandt said.
Meanwhile, Palm Beach County's population reached an estimated 1.58 million residents in July 2025, an increase of 5.6% since April 2020, according to the U.S. Census Bureau.
Brandt said new office developments in West Palm Beach and Palm Beach Gardens have made it easier for companies to establish a presence in the region.
"Florida has just been a really easy landing place," she said.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
South Florida has drawn a multitude of billionaires and corporations in recent years, buoyed by tax advantages and a booming finance and tech scene. (Eva Marie Uzcategui/Bloomberg/Getty Images)
Beyond business opportunities, Brandt pointed to year-round outdoor activities, warm weather and family life as major attractions for newcomers.
For Brandt, the region's evolution is far from complete.
"Palm Beach County, I think we're like in beginning stages of what's possible here," she said.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Americans clash over Supreme Court expansion as fight over 9 justices heats up: ‘Let’s pack it now’
summary: Americans on Capitol Hill share divided views on SCOTUS expansion, court packing, and term limits as lawmakers debate the Supreme Court's future.
story: Americans interviewed on Capitol Hill were split over whether the Supreme Court of the United States should expand as Congress introduces proposals to make reforms to its current size. (Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)

As lawmakers spar over whether to expand the U.S. Supreme Court beyond nine justices, Americans interviewed by Fox News Digital on Capitol Hill had competing views on whether the nation's highest court needs a shake-up at all.
"If it's not broken, don't fix it," Tim from Washington, D.C., told Fox News Digital.
"If you had more justices, you could have more differing opinions there," Derek, also from Washington, said. "So you'd have to have more of a consensus on whatever they're voting on."

The debate comes after a Republican-backed constitutional amendment to permanently fix the court at nine justices failed in the House in September, falling short of the two-thirds majority required for passage.
MORNING GLORY: DSA DEMOCRATS' RADICAL PLAN TO RESHAPE AMERICA STARTS WITH THE SUPREME COURT
Americans sound off on whether to expand the U.S. Supreme Court beyond nine justices. (Olivier Douliery/AFP via Getty Images, File)
Democratic lawmakers have also introduced proposals to reshape the court, including legislation to expand its membership, establish term limits and impose additional ethics requirements.
" If we're gonna change the size, we need to do it now," said Carl from Texas. "If you're going to pack the court, let's pack it now."
One person Fox News Digital spoke with questioned the motives behind efforts to increase the number of justices.

"I think those who want to increase the size, maybe just have a bias to it, if it be Republican or Democrat," Tim said about the idea of expanding the number of justices. "I say just leave it as it is, man."
JOHN YOO: THE LEFT'S SUPREME COURT PANIC COLLAPSES UNDER THE WEIGHT OF THE FACTS
Americans sound off on whether to expand the U.S. Supreme Court beyond nine justices. (Nicholas Ballasy for Fox News Digital)
Democrats have become increasingly angry over many of the court’s votes, and many have alleged their rulings to be rooted in politics rather than law.
"The more people weigh in, the more accurate the results would be, right?" an interviewee said.
One also argued that while he would be in favor of potentially expanding the Supreme Court, it would be dependent on how many additional justices were to be added.
"It depends on how much more they add," Derek said. "One or two more doesn't seem like it's that much, but if they're like, ‘Double it.’ Well, starting to just kind of go overboard at that point."
REPUBLICANS SOUND ALARM OVER HIDDEN MIDTERM STAKES THAT COULD RESHAPE SUPREME COURT FOR DECADES
U.S. Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, introduced legislation to expand the bench from nine to 13 justices. (Alex Wong/Getty Images, File)

Several proposals by Democrats have been introduced to reshape the court, including legislation from Rep. Al Green, D-Texas, to expand the bench from nine to 13 justices, and a separate measure from Rep. Ro Khanna, D-Calif., to establish 18-year terms of active service for newly appointed justices.

"I think that more substantial change would be putting in term limits," Mark from Washington, D.C., said. "The size would allow for the next several presidents to appoint more people. I don't know that it changes the political bent of the current situation, whereas a term limits might be more effective."
Other Democratic proposals would impose enforceable ethics standards and require greater transparency surrounding the court's emergency rulings, often referred to as its "shadow docket."
Republicans argue Democrats’ proposals to overhaul the Supreme Court are a reaction to the party’s anger at rulings not being in their favor.
LIBERAL JUSTICE HAMMERS SUPREME COURT FOR FAST-TRACKING EMERGENCY DOCKET CASES
House Republicans sought to permanently cap the court at nine justices, casting their proposed constitutional amendment to reject Democratic efforts to expand the court.

It failed to secure the required two-thirds majority needed to pass the House. Amending the Constitution would then also require a two-thirds majority vote in the Senate and then ratification by three-fourths of the states.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Article III, Section 1 of the Constitution establishes the Supreme Court but does not specify how many justices should serve on it, leaving Congress with the authority to determine its size.

Congress initially established six seats under the Judiciary Act of 1789. The court's size changed several times throughout the 19th century, reaching as many as 10 justices before Congress established the current nine-justice structure in 1869.
Hannah is a Production Assistant for the Politics team at Fox News Digital.

title: Senate Republican settles six-year-old campaign bill after being called out on social media
summary: After the founder of Holly's Sweet Treats called out Sen. Roger Marshall's campaign for stiffing her company on a 2020 purchase, the debt was paid off.
story: Following newly released text messages from Dr. Anthony Fauci showing private concerns over vaccine miscarriage risks, Sen. Roger Marshall demands a special counsel to investigate the former NIAID director. Marshall emphasizes that Congress can only expose the truth, while a special counsel has the power to prosecute.

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., paid a six-year-old campaign bill after a bakery owner called him out on social media for allegedly failing to pay for cookies and other treats ordered for a 2020 election watch party.

Holly Thomas, a bakery founder, said in an Oct. 8 Facebook post that she would never vote for Marshall because his campaign had failed to pay a $678.75 bill despite her repeated attempts to collect the money.
Thomas shared an image of the invoice and a photo that appeared to show custom cookies made for Marshall's campaign.

"Do you know why I will never vote for Roger Marshall? Because six years ago, when I was a brand-new small business owner, his campaign ordered cookies and treats from my bakery for his primary election watch party. And I never got paid. For nearly a year, I made repeated attempts to collect payment, reaching out by phone and email. I never received a return phone call, and the invoice was never paid," Thomas wrote in the post.
SLEEPER SENATE RACE EMERGES AS UNEXPECTED HEADACHE FOR REPUBLICANS AHEAD OF MIDTERMS
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., arrives in the U.S. Capitol for the first vote of the week on Tuesday, Sept. 22, 2026. (Bill Clark/CQ-Roll Call, Inc via Getty Images)

"Not only was I just starting out, but we were also in the middle of COVID, when small businesses everywhere were struggling just to keep their doors open. Every single dollar mattered. Those cookies and treats cost money to make, employees' time to prepare, and resources that my little business couldn't afford to give away," she explained.

"Six years later, I haven't forgotten. This isn't about political parties or policy disagreements. It's about my personal experience as a small business owner and the importance of honoring financial commitments. That experience is why Roger Marshall will never get my vote," Thomas concluded.

Marshall — who had been serving in the U.S. House of Representatives when he won election to the U.S. Senate in 2020 — addressed the issue on Oct. 10, sharing a screenshot showing a $1,300 payment to the establishment.
GOP SENATOR ALLEGES SCHUMER BEHIND 'HIT JOB' REPORT ON FORMER PATIENTS

Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., during a Senate Health, Education, Labor, and Pensions Committee confirmation hearing in Washington, D.C., on Wednesday, Sept. 16, 2026. (Daniel Heuer/Bloomberg via Getty Images)

"As some folks may have seen, there was a post on social media regarding an unpaid 2020 cookie bill. We have absolutely no idea how this happened, but rest assured as soon as it became known to us, we immediately attempted to contact the business in order to apologize, and we have repaid the bill from 2020, double," Marshall's post on X noted.
POWERFUL UNION LEADER BACKS REPUBLICAN IN KEY SENATE SHOWDOWN
Sen. Roger Marshall, R-Kan., listens as U.S. Vice President JD Vance speaks during an event at Webco Manufacturing on Sept. 14, 2026, in Olathe, Kan. (Mark Schiefelbein-Pool/Getty Images)
Thomas confirmed that the bill had been paid.

"But I can officially confirm that Roger Marshall has paid his bill! Better late than never, right? Six years later, I guess we can finally mark that invoice PAID!" she wrote in part of a Facebook post. "Thank you all for the overwhelming support! Now, back to doing what I do best!"

Marshall is seeking re-election this year.
Alex Nitzberg is a writer for Fox News Digital.

title: EXCLUSIVE: Inside LA's homeless hellscape — unlikely critics blast Dems as GOP hopeful tours Skid Row
summary: Steve Hilton walked through Skid Row's homeless encampments, accusing California's Democratic leaders of fueling the crisis with billions in spending.
story: Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton discusses homelessness, taxpayer spending and Democratic leadership during a tour of Skid Row with Fox News Digital.

LOS ANGELES — Surrounded by sprawling homeless encampments, drug use and trash-strewn sidewalks in the heart of Los Angeles' Skid Row, Republican gubernatorial candidate Steve Hilton blasted California's homelessness crisis as a "political scandal," accusing Democratic leaders of spending billions in taxpayer dollars while allowing the streets to deteriorate.

"'The homelessness crisis,' as if it's some kind of natural disaster that can't be helped," Hilton told Fox News Digital, referring to how politicians and others describe the conditions as he surveyed the sprawling encampments.
"No, it is not a crisis. It's actually a scandal. It's a political scandal because the people in charge, they've caused this with their policies."

Skid Row, the epicenter of California's homelessness crisis, is facing renewed scrutiny after a sweeping federal drug raid Thursday. The crackdown came as voting gets underway in the Nov. 3 governor's race, with Hilton challenging Democrat Xavier Becerra in a contest where homelessness and billions in taxpayer spending have emerged, yet again, as key campaign issues.
HOUSING FIRST IS A DISASTER. I SAW SACRAMENTO'S HOMELESS CHAOS FIRSTHAND
Fox News Digital visits Skid Row on Oct. 9. (Ashley J. DiMella / Fox News Digital)
'A real crony game'

Fox News Digital observed sprawling homeless encampments, Narcan distribution points, human feces on sidewalks and piles of ash from what people in the neighborhood said were fires lit earlier that morning to keep warm.

Hilton accused years of Democratic leadership of failing to solve California's homelessness problem despite billions in taxpayer spending, while taking aim at government-funded nonprofits and developers he claims have financially benefited from the crisis.

"The real estate developers, and it's a real crony game now, which I've been told about many times," he continued. "We've got a small number of real estate developers who are in on this, and they get all the contracts to build these apartment units for people that don't help them at all, because the other part of it isn't being done in terms of drug addiction or whatever."
TAXPAYER-FUNDED 'METH MANSION' UNDER FIRE AS CRIME CONCERNS MOUNT AROUND HOMELESS CAMPUS
Fox News Digital visits Skid Row on Oct. 9. (Ashley J. DiMella / Fox News Digital)

"The point about these nonprofits is that they're part of this philosophy, the ideology of harm reduction, all the things we've talked about, which means that they are not actually trying to solve the problem," Hilton said. "Because if they solve the problem, they don't get paid anymore. So they have an incentive to keep it going."

In September, federal prosecutors charged the founder of a Los Angeles-area homelessness nonprofit with wire fraud, alleging he misused taxpayer funds, including nearly $50,000 for a trip to Tahiti, after receiving more than $118 million in public funding through government contracts.

Federal and local authorities, including the FBI, DEA and LAPD, arrested 23 of 28 defendants charged in a sweeping drug trafficking investigation Thursday, targeting alleged gang-affiliated dealers and independent operators accused of selling fentanyl, methamphetamine and other drugs in and around Skid Row.
Hilton argued that addressing homelessness begins with enforcing existing laws and removing encampments from California's streets.
KAREN BASS GRILLED OVER BROKEN HOMELESSNESS PROMISE, BLAMES BUREAUCRACY FOR SLOWED PROGRESS
Shots of Skid Row seen on Oct. 9, 2026. (Ashley J. DiMella / Fox News Digital)
"My plan is very simple. How we get clean streets in California. Number one, enforce the law, get people off the streets," he said.

"Letting people live like this, and not just the people who live like this, but all the people who aren't living like this who have to experience this every single day. The collapse of civilized life in their city," Hilton said. "It's the opposite, it's cruel."
'I like being on drugs'
As Hilton walked through Skid Row with Fox News Digital, one woman living on the streets offered a candid admission about her drug use.
LA REAL ESTATE VET COMES AT MAYOR BASS WITH RECEIPTS OVER DAMNING HOMELESSNESS REPORT: 'SHE DOESN'T GET IT'
Shots of Skid Row seen on Oct. 9, 2026. (Ashley J. DiMella / Fox News Digital)
"I like being on drugs, but if I have to quit, then I most definitely will," she told Hilton when he asked whether she wanted to stop using drugs.

The woman, who said she had been living on Skid Row for five years, described moving to Los Angeles from Syracuse, New York, in part because she had heard about California's methadone clinics. She also said a former boyfriend had planned to find housing.
"I heard about the methadone clinics," she explained, saying she wanted access to methadone treatment.

Despite her admission about drug use, the woman said she was considering entering a treatment program in Tarzana, where she had heard patients could stay for a year or longer and receive methadone twice a day.
STEVE HILTON LAUNCHES AD MOCKING XAVIER BECERRA'S '36 YEARS' AS A CAREER POLITICIAN IN CALIFORNIA GOV RACE
Shots of Skid Row seen on Oct. 9, 2026. (Ashley J. DiMella / Fox News Digital)

Venus, a Skid Row volunteer who helps distribute food, blasted Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass over the handling of homelessness, even as Bass joined local law enforcement officials Thursday to announce the results of a sweeping drug crackdown in the neighborhood.
"We all loved her from the beginning, but she lied about the homeless," Venus said, pointing to the conditions surrounding her on Skid Row. "What is going on, Mayor Bass? We voted for you."
Venus later added, "She didn't do her job," and said Bass’ pledge was "getting rid of the homeless. She never did nothing. Nothing, nothing at all. Shame on her."
Hilton also took aim at his Democratic opponent, Becerra, accusing the longtime politician of taking California voters for granted while failing to offer solutions to the state's mounting problems.

"If you can't be bothered to earn people's vote, then you don't deserve people's votes. He's not campaigning. He's backing out of every single debate. I mean, I've never seen anything like it. It's complete contempt for the voters and for California," said Hilton.

Hilton, a former Fox News host, argued that Californians are growing fed up with years of Democratic leadership, pointing to homelessness, high taxes and the soaring cost of living as reasons voters may be ready for a change.

"I know everyone says, well, it's California, Republican can't win. I don't know. I think people are sick of all this," Hilton said. "And they're sick of Becerra just taking them for granted, and I think we can win this election."
'I'm a patriotic American communist'
On Skid Row, Fox News Digital encountered criticism of Democratic leadership from an unlikely political perspective: a man who described himself as a "patriotic American communist."
TRUMP ADMINISTRATION YANKS FUNDING FROM LA HOMELESS AGENCY AMID EXPLOSIVE FRAUD PROBE: 'NECESSARY STEP'
Fox News Digital spoke with volunteers on Skid Row. (Ashley J. DiMella / Fox News Digital)
The man, who identified himself as Adrian, said he had moved from Orange County and ended up on Skid Row following a medical incident.
"I'm a patriotic American communist, part of the American Communist Party," Adrian said.
Adrian said he belonged to the American Communist Party, distancing himself from the mainstream Democratic Party.
Asked whether California's leaders were doing enough to address homelessness, Adrian was blunt.
"Oh, definitely not. I have to be honest, I'm a leftist, and so the Democratic Party isn't for me. I'm more left than they are," he said.

Adrian said he had been living on Skid Row for about a year after being evicted from a medical facility, and now volunteers at the Skid Row Care Campus, which he credited with providing therapy, medical services and community activities.

"It gives them better things to do than just do drugs all day," he said.
Fox News Digital reached out to Becerra's campaign and Los Angeles Mayor Karen Bass' office for comment.

title: Blue-state governor’s race defies expectations as Republican closes in: Power Rankings
summary: Christine Drazan aims to end Oregon's four-decade GOP losing streak in a tight rematch with Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek over local issues.
story: Oregon Republican gubernatorial nominee Christine Drazan, in a Fox News Digital interview, targets Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek over economy, homelessness, in a high-stakes rematch

Republicans are gaining ground in blue-leaning Oregon, where Fox News Power Rankings have shifted the governor's race toward the GOP as Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek faces a competitive rematch with Republican Christine Drazan.

The shift from Likely Democrat to Lean Democrat reflects a competitive political environment in Oregon, where concerns over homelessness, housing, taxes, schools and the cost of living have created an opening for Republicans to end a more than four-decade losing streak in gubernatorial elections.

Republicans are gaining ground in Oregon even as they face a rough national political environment marked by high gas and diesel prices, what polls show is an unpopular war in Iran and President Donald Trump's low approval ratings.
"This is something historic we're trying to pull off," Drazan said in a Fox News Digital interview. "It's been a long time, and we're due we win."
CHECK OUT THE LATEST FOX NEWS POWER RANKINGS IN THE MIDTERM ELECTIONS
Fox News Power Rankings on gubernatorial forecast. (Remy Numa/Fox News)
Then-Vice President Kamala Harris carried Oregon by 14 points in the 2024 presidential election, and Democratic Sen. Ron Wyden won his 2022 re-election by 15 points.
But gubernatorial showdowns in the northwestern state have traditionally been much closer contests.
Drazan, a former GOP leader in the Oregon House, lost to Kotek by less than four points in 2022.
After her defeat, she won a state House election in 2024 and returned to the legislature, serving again as minority leader before being appointed last year to the state Senate.

"It's good to stay in the fight. I think Oregonians ... recognized that I didn't leave, I didn't move to a different state, I didn't go hide. I got engaged again, went back into the legislature to serve my community," Drazan emphasized. "I think that that matters to people, that I am committed long-term to our state."
The latest public opinion polls indicate a margin of error race in the Kotek-Drazan rematch.

"People are starting to get to know me a little bit more and my leadership, and they're taking a closer look at whether or not Oregon is uniquely bad right now. It's not a national issue, it's here at home," Drazan said. "We're struggling right now locally. So, that's making this race tight."
While Drazan is trying to keep her focus on Oregon and local issues, the Kotek campaign is aiming to anchor the GOP challenger to Trump, who is very unpopular in the state.
DEMOCRATS THINK A BLUE WAVE IS FORMER - HERE ARE THREE FACTORS THAT COULD STOP IT
Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek of Oregon, who is running for re-election in 2026, is facing off in a rematch with Republican Christine Drazan. (Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images)

Kotek communications director Federico Araujo told Fox News Digital, "There are still many undecided voters ahead of November. But when the choice is clear in an election, they always show up. And the choice couldn't be any clearer in this race: Christine Drazan is ready to open the door to Trump's agenda and Governor Kotek is fighting every day to protect Oregonians from federal overreach and harm."
But Drazan said that "Oregon needs change. Oregon needs to be done with one approach to the world. Single-party control has not been good for us in my home state. And we need that balance."

"We need people to be at the table that have been ignored in the past to be able to turn our economy around, frankly, and turn our schools around and serve the people that are facing addiction and slowly dying on our streets. Those are significant challenges, and Tina Kotek doesn't have the answers to solve them," she charged.
Four years ago, Drazan received plenty of support from national Republicans as her party benefited from a more favorable political environment.
DEMOCRACY ’26: STAY UP TO DATE WITH THE FOX NEWS ELECTION HUB

Oregon State Sen. Christine Drazan is the Republican nominee for a second straight cycle, as she challenges Democratic Gov. Tina Kotek in a rematch of their 2022 showdown. (Photo by Mathieu Lewis-Rolland/Getty Images)

This time around, national Republicans are facing stiff headwinds as they work to hang on to their fragile congressional majorities and governors' offices across the country. But the Drazan campaign says it's now landing financial support from the Republican Governors Association.
"I am grateful to have the Republican Governors Association as a partner in this race. They are investing in this race now," Drazan said.
But she noted "the sitting governor has a fundraising advantage that's significant today," and added, "I could always use more support."

Democratic Governors Association spokesperson Johanna Warshaw spotlighted the competitive nature of the Oregon gubernatorial showdowns, but told Fox News Digital, "Governor Kotek has the advantage, and we're confident she'll win.
"Clearly, the RGA agrees as they're leaving Christine Drazan's broke campaign out to dry," Warshaw claimed.

Drazan highlighted that she's "actively fundraising all the time and encouraging folks to get involved in this race right now. We have no limits in Oregon, and that allows me to be able to compete head to head."
And pointing to her campaign, she said, "I want to achieve something extraordinary."
Paul Steinhauser covers the national campaign trail from coast to coast for Fox News

title: Trump and Rubio weigh firing Kimberly Guilfoyle as misconduct and donor bailout allegations mount
summary: Kimberly Guilfoyle faces mounting allegations in Greece as JD Vance and Marco Rubio weigh in on the embattled ambassador's growing controversies.
story: Fox News Flash top headlines are here. Check out what's clicking on FoxNews.com.

U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle may soon be fired amid reports she sought a six-figure credit card bailout from a Trump donor while offering access to administration officials, adding to mounting allegations over her conduct in Athens.

President Donald Trump and Secretary of State Marco Rubio are "extremely pissed off" by Guilfoyle’s reported conduct and are weighing her removal, The Associated Press reported Sunday, citing a senior U.S. official.
The official told the AP that a decision on what action to take would likely come this week after Monday’s Columbus Day holiday. No departure has been confirmed.

Guilfoyle, onetime fiancée of Donald Trump Jr., came under scrutiny this week after The Wall Street Journal reported that she asked Trump donor Eric Deters to pay off a $100,000 American Express bill shortly before her Senate confirmation hearing.
MARCO RUBIO ANNOUNCES SWEEPING FINANCIAL SANCTIONS AGAINST THE INTERNATIONAL CRIMINAL COURT

US Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle (R) attends the opening of the sixth round of the Greece-US Strategic Dialogue, in Athens, on October 7, 2026. (Photo by Mark Schiefelbein / POOL / AFP via Getty Images)

According to messages reviewed by the Journal, Guilfoyle urged Deters to wire the money directly to American Express, saying the transaction would not leave a paper trail, while offering to help him gain access to senior Trump administration officials. Deters said he never made the payment.
Guilfoyle's attorney, Jesse Binnall, disputed the authenticity of the messages.

The allegations followed an earlier Journal investigation into Guilfoyle's conduct in Greece, including claims that she promoted the interests of Greek construction and energy company Aktor Group and allowed its registered lobbyist, Christos Marafatsos, to accompany her to private diplomatic meetings with senior officials.
FORMER TRUMP CABINET OFFICIAL HAD 'INAPPROPRIATELY CLOSE' RELATIONSHIP WITH BODYGUARD, IG FINDS

The Journal also reported that Guilfoyle suggested at a dinner with Greek officials that the U.S. would undermine their government, citing political developments in Romania. Greece's foreign minister has since said there was no need to summon Guilfoyle for an explanation because the country's energy minister denied that any threat had been made.

Separately, the State Department's Office of Inspector General opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees, private travel, acceptance of gifts and relationships with business interests, according to a report from the Daily Mail.
3 SECRET SERVICE OFFICIALS UNDER INTERNAL INVESTIGATION FOR POTENTIAL MISCONDUCT

FILE - The State Department's Office of Inspector General reportedly opened an investigation into allegations involving Guilfoyle's treatment of embassy employees. (Photo by Jacek Boczarski/Anadolu via Getty Images)

Sources described a hostile workplace in which Guilfoyle allegedly threatened to fire employees. They also claim that she demoted members of her security detail over minor incidents, including an officer who reportedly failed to answer a 4 a.m. request for ice while she was vacationing in Mykonos.
The inspector general's office declined to confirm or deny the existence of an investigation. Binnall told the Daily Mail that "any implication of wrongdoing by the Ambassador is unsupported."

The allegations have drawn scrutiny from congressional Democrats, including Sen. Jeanne Shaheen, D-N.H., and Rep. Gregory Meeks, D-N.Y., who have called for a review of Guilfoyle's conduct. Meeks urged her removal if the allegations were substantiated.
Vice President JD Vance addressed the controversy Friday, cautioning against rushing to judgment while acknowledging that misconduct should carry consequences.
OHIO BAKERY WORKERS RECOUNT SURPRISE JD VANCE ENCOUNTER THAT TOOK AN UNEXPECTED TURN

"Let's actually see what the facts are. Let's see what the truth is," Vance told reporters in Ohio. "And obviously, if there was something bad that happened, then people have to suffer consequences for it."
Secretary of State Marco Rubio, who visited Greece this week and delivered remarks with the backdrop of Acropolis, declined to address the allegations directly.
SEC MARCO RUBIO: THE WEST FORGOT WHAT MADE IT GREAT. WE MUST REDISCOVER OUR ROOTS BEFORE WE LOSE THEM
"You guys walk around thinking that because some source told you something and you reported it, it's the gospel. It's not the gospel," Rubio told reporters Thursday.
Rubio had defended Guilfoyle's performance a day earlier, saying, "Our ambassador has been a strong ambassador here."
FOUR AMERICAN TOURISTS AMONG 6 KILLED AFTER EXPLOSION LEVELS BUILDING NEAR ATHENS’ ACROPOLIS

Republican vice presidential candidate, U.S. Sen. J.D. Vance (R-OH) speaks to Donald Trump Jr. (L) as Kimberly Guilfoyle looks on, during preparations for the second day of the Republican National Convention at the Fiserv Forum on July 16, 2024 in Milwaukee, Wisconsin.  (Getty Images)

Trump nominated Guilfoyle to the diplomatic post in December 2024. A former California prosecutor and Fox News Channel personality, she previously served as a prominent surrogate and fundraiser for the president.
DONALD TRUMP JR AND BETTINA ANDERSON CELEBRATE PRIVATE WEDDING IN BAHAMAS, SHARE SWEET PERSONAL PHOTO

Guilfoyle was almost Trump’s daughter-in-law. She was engaged to Don Jr. for four years, but the two publicly split in Dec. 2024 — the same month the president nominated her to be the ambassador to Greece.
The president’s eldest son married Palm Beach socialite Bettina Anderson in May of this year.
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
She was also previously married to California Gov. Gavin Newsom, a Democrat, from 2001 to 2006, when he was serving as mayor of San Francisco.

title: Quiet part out loud: Anti-Israel mobs want one state called 'Palestine,' erasing Israel
summary: Three pro-Palestinian activists tell Fox News Digital they envision replacing Israel with a single democratic state, with one proposing the name "1948."
story: Fox News Digital spoke with three figures at a pro-Palestinian demonstration in Washington, D.C., asking each to lay out their vision for the future for Israelis and Palestinians.

WASHINGTON, D.C. — This weekend, millions of anti-Israel activists marched through the streets of cities in coordinated actions from America's capital to London, Paris, Madrid and Kuala Lumpar, Malaysia, chanting the familiar refrains of "Free, free Palestine" and "From the river to the sea, Palestine will be free."

But for the first time, communicated frankly in exclusive interviews with Fox News Digital, three anti-Israel leaders acknowledged the goal: one state called "Palestine" encompassing modern-day Israel, the West Bank and Gaza, with a Palestinian "right of return" to the new country and equal political, voting and citizenship rights for Palestinians alongside Jews currently living in Israel.
Most significantly, in the political vision they described, Israel would legally cease to exist as a separate Jewish nation-state and Jews would be quickly overwhelmed demographically.
INSIDE THE PROTEST PLAYBOOK TO VILIFY ISRAEL ON 'GLOBAL DAY OF ACTION'
Protestors march at an anti-Israel protest in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

The current population of Israel is about 10 million, including about 7.8 million Jews, 2 million Palestinian Arabs (including Palestinians and most of them Muslim), and 200,000 people from other communities. There are another estimated 10.2 million Jews worldwide.
There are about 5.5 million Palestinians in the West Bank and Gaza and about 8 million Palestinians in the diaspora, totaling about 13.5 million.

The candor of the anti-Israel leaders lays bare the political conclusion of an argument that activists have spent years advancing on the streets, through sympathetic media outlets and in legal forums: that Israel is a "settler colonial" state practicing "apartheid" and "genocide," and therefore should not continue to exist in its current form as a Jewish state. Israeli leaders have fiercely rejected those allegations, disputing accusations of "genocide" and "apartheid" and maintaining that Israel is the nation-state of the Jewish people with equal civil and political rights for citizens that include Jews, Christians and Muslims.

Advocates for Israel note that the nation's critics rarely apply the same historical lens of human-rights analysis to Arab and Muslim-majority states, many of which emerged from the collapse of empires, wars and population upheavals that displaced millions, including Jews expelled from their countries, today often restricting political, religious and minority rights.
NOBEL PEACE PRIZE AWARDED TO UN JURIST WHO ACCUSED ISRAEL OF COMMITTING GENOCIDE IN GAZA

In Chicago, Hatem Abudayyeh, the Palestinian-American founder of the U.S. Palestinian Community Network and a Muslim, said the new nation would be "one democratic secular state of Palestine." Jewish Israeli-born community leader Miko Peled, founder of the Palestine House in Washington, D.C., said "the proper name would be Palestine." And Maryland congressional candidate Sam Husseini, a Palestinian-American Christian, floated another name for the vision of the one state: "1948," marking the year Israel declared independence and Palestinians commemorate as the "Nakba," or catastrophe, but he said even Israeli Jews would one day accept another name: "Palestine."

Their answers provide a striking interpretation from inside a movement where activists have traditionally danced around their demands with euphemisms about "liberation" and media outlets have obscured their answers even when they have been transparent.

On Washington, D.C.'s First Avenue SE, Fox News Digital asked Olivia DiNucci, local coordinator for CodePink, a far-left nonprofit, what her group sees as a solution to the Israeli-Palestinian conflict. In her work for CodePink, DiNucci disrupts hearings, restaurant meals and town halls to shout at lawmakers and policymakers who support the state of Israel.
Olivia DiNucci, D.C. coordinator at CodePink, marches at an anti-Israel protest in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)
‘TROJAN HORSES’ IN AMERICA: CONGRESS PROBES INFLUENCE NETWORKS TIED TO CHINA, IRAN AND CUBA
"Palestinians in Palestine will decide, DiNucci said.
Asked if "Palestine" includes modern day Israel, she spun around and walked away. Later, she posted a message on social media, saying she was asked "gotcha questions."
This weekend, protesters signaled their position with certainty, explicitly rejecting the two-state solution that has dominated international diplomacy for decades.
In New York City, the Party for Socialism and Liberation circulated video of protesters marching through the streets chanting: "1-2-3-4. Occupation no more. 5-6-7-8. Israel is a terrorist state."
ISRAEL, JEWS TARGETED WORLDWIDE AS WELL-FUNDED LEFTIST, ISLAMIST GROUPS JOIN FOR ‘NAKBA 78’ PROTESTS
Then came the point: "We don't want no two state!"
In London, the Palestine Solidarity Campaign promoted a 15-second video of a woman with a megaphone shouting: "There is only one state!"
"Palestine, '48!" protesters responded.
"Say it loud, say it clear!" she continued. "Palestine, you make us proud!"

Back in Washington, D.C., protesters carried signs declaring, "LAND YOU HAVE 2 KILL FOR IS NOT YOURS," a message that challenged Israel's claim to the land itself, while a banner proclaiming, "THE FIGHT FOR LIBERATION IS OURS," framed the struggle as one for the territory. The demonstrators yesterday didn't address the Hamas attacks on Israel on Oct. 7, 2023, but many have called them justified.
ANTI-ISRAEL GROUPS RALLY ACROSS US ON OCTOBER 7 ANNIVERSARY, CHANTING 'LONG LIVE THE INTIFADA'
Protestors march at an anti-Israel protest in Washington, D.C., on Oct. 10, 2026. (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)

The one-state demand is being amplified within a powerful protest infrastructure. The broader "red-green" alliance brings socialist and communist groups together on the streets with Palestinian and Muslim activist organizations, while organizations including the Democratic Socialists of America and nonprofits in the network funded by Neville Roy Singham, an American-born tech tycoon living in Shanghai, help organize, promote and amplify anti-Israel demonstrations.

Singham, has poured $278 million into a pro-communist network, including CodePink, the People's Forum, the Party for Socialism and Liberation, BreakThrough News and the ANSWER Coalition, which have become major organizing, media and logistical hubs for the protest movement. The result is a powerful infrastructure amplifying slogans such as "Free Palestine" and "from the river to the sea," even when the organizations and activists doing the amplifying don't themselves explicitly spell out the one-state political vision described to Fox News Digital.

From Chicago, Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital that the U.S. Palestinian Community Network advocates for one democratic state across the territory that today encompasses Israel, the West Bank and Gaza.
"Our points of unity, from the very beginning of our existence, included one democratic secular state of Palestine," he said.

"And for decades and decades, we've been saying that...the only true solution that can bring peace and justice to all that live there is ... one democratic state," which includes the West Bank, Gaza and "1948 Palestinian territories," a term used to describe the land that Israel claimed as a nation in 1948.
This can only happen, he said, if "the racist system of Zionism is dismantled."

The ADL, a leading Jewish organization based in New York, describes Zionism as a "movement for the self-determination and statehood for the Jewish people in their ancestral homeland, the land of Israel."

Women at an anti-Israel rally on Oct. 9, 2026, in Kuala Lumpur, Malaysia, hold placards reading messages created by the leaders of the Global Alliance for Palestine for protests around the country. The messages read "Humanity Is Not a Crime," "Let Gaza Live" and "Stop the Genocide War." (Annice Lyn/Getty Images)
Abudayyeh said the new state would include a "right of return" for Palestinian refugees and their descendants. "Our points of unity from day one included the right of return," he said.

Activists from a U.S.-based network of groups called "Al-Awda: The Palestine Right to Return Coalition" joined the protest in Los Angeles and posted a message online: "OUR PEOPLE WILL RETURN, PALESTINE WILL BE FREE!

"If all of our refugees, who have the internationally recognized right to return to Palestine, are able to return, and the system, the racist system is dismantled, then all the people there can live in peace and justice," Abudayyeh told Fox News Digital. "That's our position. It's always been our position. We're not going to abandon the five to seven million refugees that we have."
Marchers protest against Israel on Oct. 10, 2026 (Brooke Curto/Fox News Digital)
"They have the right to go back to the homes and lands in which they were exiled," he explained.
Abudayyeh said that wouldn't mean removing the people – most of them Jewish – living in Israel.

"It doesn't mean that we're going to kick people out," he said. "It just means that these folks have an internationally recognized right, and you will never get peace and justice there unless you uphold that right."

"I believe, very clearly, USPCN believes very clearly that there can be peace and justice as long as that system, that racist system of Zionism is dismantled," Abudayyeh said. "That's the essence of it."

Abudayyeh compared the Palestinian movement's objective to the international campaign against apartheid South Africa. "And we're getting close to having international consensus today on the question of Israel and Zionism, where Israel doesnt have the "right to exist as a racist, Zionist, apartheid, white supremacist state."
"That's what we say," he continued. "We're adamant about that. We're clear about it. Unabashed."
Fox News Digital asked Abudayyeh whether "Palestine" includes modern-day Israel when protest leaders and activists chant "Palestine will be free" or "Free, free Palestine."
"The majority of the majority of the people, especially in the past period, have moved to that conclusion," Abudayyeh said.

Husseini, a Palestinian-American journalist running for Congress in Maryland's 4th Congressional District, offered a similar one-state vision and an unusual proposal for what the country might be called.

Standing on First Avenue SE, between the U.S. Supreme Court and the U.S. Capitol, Husseini told Fox News Digital that his long-term vision is "one person, one vote," coupled with a Palestinian right of return.
"Ultimately, long-term, I that it should be one person, one vote," Husseini said.

"Why aren't they allowed back into their homes? So I think that they should," he said of Palestinian refugees. "I mean, that includes myself. I don't know that I would actually move back there, but as a descendant of a Palestinian who was forcibly displaced, I should have that right or compensation."
Husseini offered another possibility for the country's name.
"I've often thought of a novel proposal because people get hung up on the names. Are they going to call it Israel or are they going call it Palestine?" Husseini said.
"I've toyed with the idea of calling it 1948, having a country with a number signifying the year of this cataclysm, which should be the last gasp of imperialism."

If the new state is called Palestine, Husseini said, "I think a lot of Jews, when they think about it, will say, so long as they have equal rights and all are protected, will adopt the term Palestine."

Standing on Pennsylvania Avenue SE, the roar of the demonstrators getting closer as they marched from the U.S. Capitol to talks at the Palestine House of Freedom, Miko Peled, an Israeli-born Jewish activist, was equally blunt about what a "Free Palestine" means to him.

"Well, our vision, our mission, and our vision is to educate people to see that a free Palestine, which means a post-Zionist, post-apartheid Palestine with equal rights and the right of the Palestinians to return, is the best vision that will benefit everybody who lives there currently, which means Israelis and Palestinians," he said.
Organizers from a coalition, Global Action for Palestine, share a map "Global Day of Action" events for 2026. (Global Alliance for Palestine)
Asked whether that meant one state, he answered yes.
"It's already one state, it's just an apartheid state," Peled said.
"So that's our vision, to create a real democracy, free Palestine, with equal rights."
Fox News Digital asked what that country would be called.

"Well, historically the country was called Palestine for thousands of years and so it should be called Palestine," Peled said. "Israel is a new name. They renamed the country 78 years ago, so the proper name would be Palestine."
For Peled, the familiar protest demand "Free Palestine" has a literal political meaning: One state with the new name "Palestine."

She is the author of "Woke Army: The Red-Green Alliance That Is Undermining America’s Freedom." She can be reached at asra.nomani@fox.com and on X at @asranomani.

title: Hurricane Isaias’ devastating aftermath comes into focus in striking images
summary: Photos and video capture the hurricane's devastating aftermath as flooded streets, damaged homes and scattered debris reveal the storm's full impact.
story: United Cajun Navy Incident Cmdr. Josh Gill joins ‘Fox News Live’ as Florida communities begin cleaning up after Hurricane Isaias left widespread damage and power outages in its wake. Gill discusses recovery efforts on the ground and how volunteers are helping residents clear debris and rebuild after the storm.
Communities are beginning to assess the damage left behind by a powerful hurricane that tore through the region, leaving homes damaged, roads flooded and neighborhoods littered with debris.
Photos from some of the hardest-hit areas show the scale of the destruction as residents and emergency crews begin the long process of cleaning up and rebuilding.
HOW THE VIOLENT CATEGORY 2 STORM UNFOLDED ACROSS FLORIDA AND GULF COAST

Copper Brock helps salvage what he can from the Milton Quick Stop after the roof was torn off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Isaias slammed into the Florida Panhandle near Destin on Friday, Oct. 9, as a Category 2 hurricane with maximum sustained winds of 105 mph, bringing destructive winds, dangerous storm surge and widespread flooding.
The hurricane tore roofs from buildings, uprooted trees and knocked out power to hundreds of thousands of customers across Florida and Alabama before pushing inland.
STUNNING FOOTAGE CAPTURES HURRICANE ISAIAS FROM INSIDE THE STORM’S EYE

In an aerial view, an apartment complex is seen after the roof was blown off when Hurricane Isaias passed through the area on October 10, 2026, in Milton, Florida. Hurricane Isaias made landfall as the season's first Atlantic hurricane with category two winds. (Joe Raedle/Getty Images)

Isaias marked the first hurricane to make landfall along the U.S. Gulf Coast since Hurricane Milton battered Florida in October 2024, nearly two years earlier.
The storm also became the first hurricane of the 2026 Atlantic season, ending an unusually quiet stretch that saw no hurricanes develop until October.

title: Rescue expert warns FlyDubai hijacking attempt shows US, allies are ‘playing checkers’ against terror threat
summary: Bryan Stern, a 9/11 first responder and rescue expert, warns the FlyDubai hijacking exposes how far behind Western counterterrorism strategy has fallen.
story: Grey Bull Rescue CEO Bryan Stern talks about global terrorism threats and warns an attack that dwarfs 9/11 could hit America if the U.S. does not learn more about its adversaries.

The FlyDubai attempted hijacking shows the U.S. and its allies are still using outdated counterterrorism assumptions against increasingly sophisticated enemies, a U.S. rescue expert and 9/11 first responder warns.

"They’re good at chess," Bryan Stern, chairman and CEO of Grey Bull Rescue, told Fox News Digital on Monday, saying the radical ideology behind the FlyDubai attack is a ringing "bell" for global aviation security and Western counterterrorism strategy.
"And we’re, if we’re lucky, playing checkers – if we’re lucky – and I would argue we’re not even playing checkers that well."
TERROR CELLS INSIDE FOREIGN AIRLINES 'CERTAINLY A POSSIBILITY,' RETIRED PILOT WARNS
Grey Bull Rescue's Bryan Stern speaks to Fox News Digital about the world guarded against the next 9/11 terrorist attack. (Fox News Digital)

Stern, whose global nonprofit conducts evacuations from war zones and hostage situations, said the thwarted FlyDubai attack by "an angry, radicalized, Sunni bad guy" is showing just how far behind our enemies we are in this post-9/11 world.

"They understand us significantly more than we understand them," Stern, who has been "hunting the bad guys" for 30 years, said. Stern said the U.S. has to understand the "asymmetric warfare" as well as the increasingly sophisticated enemy does.
"The reason why a football coach watches game tapes is not to watch his own team play, it's to watch the bad guys play," he said. "We gotta start watching some game tapes."
AMERICA BUILT A FORTRESS AFTER 9/11. THEN THE THREAT STARTED HIDING IN PLAIN SIGHT
Captain Smit Machchhar, the Indian pilot who was attacked on a FlyDubai plane heading to Israel last week, has been hailed globally as a hero. (Israel Foreign Ministry)
Stern is intimately in tune with the playbook on the ground in war zones, including the Middle East and Iran.

"We conduct these operations in these places still to this very day," he said. "We're actually on the ground, meaning I know people in Hezbollah, I know people in the Taliban. I know people in ISIS. I know people in ISIS-K. I've met with radical jihadi weirdos and whack jobs personally."

United Arab Emirates investigators have described the incident aboard FlyDubai flight FZ1073 as an attempted terror attack after the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the captain and tried to hijack the plane, which was carrying more than 170 passengers and crew, most of them Israelis. Australian authorities have also said a counterterrorism unit is investigating the co-pilot’s links to Australia.
INTEL CHIEF WARNS OF 'EVOLVING' THREATS AS TERROR GROUPS NOW 'RECRUIT THEIR AGENTS ONLINE'
"The bad guys are completely not afraid. They're completely emboldened. They have got the whole world to hate Israel, the whole world to hate us," he said. "It's a tough problem."

Since the incident, there has been renewed vigilance in aviation and foreign airline security. Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu instructed his national security council to review security procedures for foreign civil aviation to Israel, while Vice President JD Vance said Monday that flight security procedures are also under review in the U.S.
IRAN COULD MOVE SHADOW WAR IN A DANGEROUS DIRECTION, EXPERTS WARN ON BACK OF TWO POSSIBLE TERROR ATTACKS
"I was asked years ago when I was still with the government," Stern said. "A team was put together and the question before the court was, if you were al-Qaeda, what would you do?"

"What I came up with was ... I would get 19 hijackers, and I would hijack four airplanes, and I would fly them into buildings in America, and then issue a communique that said: 20 years of war, you are no safer today than you were before – that for TSA, and Homeland Security, and Iraq, and Afghanistan and all the different things, you are actually no safer, America, today than you were before," he said.
"We're seeing, sadly," he lamented, "that academic hypothetical situation has now become a reality, or certainly a possibility."

Despite President Donald Trump and the War Department's best efforts to rid the world of terrorist groups – and Iran of nuclear weapons aspirations – "you can't bomb your way into peace," Stern claimed.
'CRAZY' FLYDUBAI LANDING EXPLAINED BY ISRAELI PILOT, WHO OFFERS STEPS TO PREVENT FUTURE CRISES
"They have been in holy war against us," he added. "We have now engaged in a holy war against them."

"On Ramadan, the holiest month of the year in Islam, on the first day, which is the holiest day, we detonated the leader of the Shia faith, the Ayatollah," he said, likening it to "if somebody assassinated the pope on Easter Sunday while he's giving mass at the Vatican."

Stern explained that rooting out ideological terror in the U.S. is more complex than ever, because even if the border is not open any longer under Trump, the terrorist networks might be infiltrating America with U.S. passport holders – making them tough to investigate, if not impossible to spot before an attack.
NETANYAHU PRAISES HEROIC BYSTANDER IN BLOODY COCKPIT ATTACK FOR PREVENTING ‘ANOTHER 9/11’
Stern likened it to the release of the suspects in the RAF Fairford investigation – potential terrorist passport holders walking free.
"Until I actually squeeze the triggers, I haven't committed a crime yet," he said. "Now give me an airplane."
"That's the problem."
Stern noted that the nature of America's adversaries in the current conflict is unlike what the U.S. faced in places like Afghanistan.

"We need to remember we are very used to shooting people like the Taliban who don't know what plumbing is – who literally for years lived in caves until we showed up and gave them stuff," he continued. "The bad guys that we're talking about today are extremely sophisticated. They are extremely resourced, extremely resourceful. They're very intelligent, they're very smart, and they're very good at what they do."
IRAN UNDER SCRUTINY AFTER PLOT FOILED NEAR UK BASE USED BY US MILITARY

"The Persian Empire is the only empire of empires who have been all the way on top and all the way defeated at the bottom – six times," he said. "They're looking at us going, you're 250 years old. How adorable. You're cute, America."
Stern predicted that some day even 9/11 — which he survived as a first responder — is ultimately going to be dwarfed.
"What will happen, probably is we'll get attacked – just like 9/11, we'll get attacked," he said. "We'll say, 'Oh my God, how did this happen?' People will wake up."

"I promise you there will come a time, it will be, you know, June 26 or whatever, where we're gonna read about 9/11, and we're gonna say, 'Wow, that wasn't so bad, only 3,000 died,'" he warned.
"Why? Because we have created a holy war. We have now gotten into the crazy. And you cannot unring that bell."

title: WATCH: CDC director discusses US government response to Russian plague concerns: 'We are protected'
summary: CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz says the agency is monitoring travelers from Siberia amid concerns about a pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia.
story: CDC Director Erica Schwartz discusses agency safety efforts amid a reported plague outbreak in Russia at WSJ's "Future of Health" summit Wednesday. (Credit: The Wall Street Journal and WSJ The Future of Health, Oct. 7)

The Centers for Disease Control and Prevention (CDC) is coordinating with federal agencies to monitor travelers entering the United States from Siberia amid concerns about a possible pneumonic plague outbreak in Russia, the agency's director revealed Wednesday.

CDC Director Dr. Erica Schwartz said the Trump administration is working across multiple agencies to identify travelers arriving from the region following the mysterious death of a Russian laboratory worker, while emphasizing that the risk to Americans remains minimal.
"We are very confident that the threat to the United States is extremely low," Schwartz said during a Wall Street Journal health forum Wednesday.
MOTHER OF DEAD RUSSIAN ANTI-PLAGUE INSTITUTE WORKER: 'I KNOW THE TRUTH'

Darya Shipilova, 28, an employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute of Siberia and the Far East, died after developing pneumonia of an unknown cause, prompting quarantines and heightened health precautions in the region. Russian authorities say testing has found no evidence her illness was linked to pathogens she worked with. (East2West news)

The concerns stem from the Oct. 2 death of Darya Shipilova, a 28-year-old employee of the Irkutsk Anti-Plague Research Institute in Siberia, whose death has fueled speculation about a possible pneumonic plague infection.
Russian authorities have maintained that Shipilova died from pneumonia of unknown origin and have not confirmed that she was infected with Yersinia pestis, the bacteria that causes pneumonic plague.
Schwartz said the CDC is working with the departments of Homeland Security, State and War, among other federal agencies, to track potential arrivals from the region.

"There are about 200 flights that come into the United States from Siberia, that region," Schwartz said, adding that those flights typically arrive at New York's John F. Kennedy International Airport.
"We have a port health station set up in JFK so that we can do appropriate surveillance and screening if anyone from that area comes into the United States," she continued.

The CDC director stressed that while pneumonic plague is a serious bacterial infection capable of spreading between people through respiratory droplets, early detection and treatment can prevent deaths.
TRUMP RESPONDS TO CONCERNS OVER SUSPECTED PLAGUE CASE IN RUSSIA, SAYING US 'WILLING TO HELP'
The Senate confirmed Dr. Erica Schwartz to be the next director of the Centers for Disease Control. (Finn Gomez/Getty Images)

"The one good thing, if I could say there's a good thing, is that it's a treatable, highly treatable bacterial disease with common antibiotics that most physicians within the United States can utilize," Schwartz said.

The illness is caused by the bacterium Yersinia pestis and is considered the most serious form of plague, according to the CDC. Symptoms can include fever, chest pain, coughing and rapidly developing pneumonia. Without prompt antibiotic treatment, the infection can be fatal, the agency warns.
The World Health Organization (WHO) has pressed Moscow for additional information about Shipilova's death.

Russian authorities placed approximately 200 people who had contact with the deceased laboratory worker under quarantine, according to Euronews. On Thursday, Irkutsk Gov. Igor Kobzev said preventive measures had been completed and roughly 5,000 laboratory tests had detected no pathogens, according to the Associated Press.
RUSSIAN RESEARCHER'S MYSTERY DEATH COULD BE ‘FAR WORSE’ THAN THE PLAGUE, FORMER SENIOR TRUMP OFFICIAL WARNS
A view of the entrance to the grounds of the anti-plague institute in the city of Irkutsk on Oct. 7, 2026. (TATYANA MAKEYEVA / AFP via Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP

However, Russian officials have not publicly identified the pathogen responsible for Shipilova's pneumonia or definitively ruled out pneumonic plague as the cause of her death, according to The Associated Press.
Asked whether Moscow was being sufficiently transparent with American authorities, Schwartz indicated that the administration was still seeking answers.
"We are still having those conversations about what exactly happened in Siberia," she said, adding that U.S. officials were working with information about an unconfirmed case of pneumonic plague.
Alec Schemmel is a Politics Reporter for Fox News Digital who is originally from Charlotte, North Carolina but now resides in the Washington D.C.-Baltimore Metro Area.

title: Trump announces immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine
summary: President Donald Trump declared an immediate energy ceasefire, but his recent deal easing Russian diesel exports drew sharp criticism from Kyiv.
story: RSM US chief economist Joe Brusuelas warned restricting diesel exports could have provided short-term relief before driving up transportation costs and grocery prices for American consumers.

President Donald Trump announced an immediate energy ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine, saying both countries have agreed to halt attacks on each other's energy infrastructure after weeks of escalating tensions over strikes on oil refineries and power plants.
"Effective immediately, there is an ENERGY CEASEFIRE in the War between Russia and Ukraine. Both parties have agreed. Do not break it!" Trump wrote on Truth Social.

The announcement comes as Trump has intensified pressure on Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy to stop targeting Russian oil refineries, arguing that the attacks have disrupted global diesel supplies and contributed to higher fuel prices for American consumers.
The issue has become increasingly urgent as diesel prices weigh on American farmers, truckers and businesses that rely on the fuel to transport goods and operate heavy equipment.
RECORD GAS PRICES SQUEEZE AMERICANS AS MIDTERMS LOOM AND WAR IN UKRAINE AND IRAN WAGES ON

Trump has repeatedly criticized Ukraine's strikes on Russian energy facilities, even as Kyiv maintains that targeting Moscow's oil industry is a legitimate strategy to weaken Russia's ability to finance its war.

The announcement follows a contentious week in U.S.-Ukraine relations after Trump struck a deal with Russian President Vladimir Putin to allow Russian diesel exports to reach American and global markets.

Under the agreement announced Friday, Russia would immediately supply more than 300,000 tons of diesel, with additional shipments expected in November and beyond. The Treasury Department also authorized temporary sanctions relief to facilitate Russian diesel supplies.
Trump argued that the agreement would help bring down fuel prices, while Zelenskyy criticized the decision as a concession to Moscow that could provide additional revenue for Russia's war effort.
The dispute escalated Saturday when Trump suggested Ukraine should replace Zelenskyy with a leader more willing to negotiate an end to the war.
"I suggest they get a new leader who can make a deal," Trump told reporters.
'OUR POSITION IS CLEAR:' ZELENSKYY AND EU DISMISS CEDING UKRAINIAN LAND TO RUSSIA

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskiy gestures next to U.S. President Donald Trump during a meeting at the Oval Office of the White House, amid negotiations to end the Russian war in Ukraine, in Washington, D.C., Aug. 18, 2025.  (Kevin Lamarque/Reuters)

Zelenskyy, meanwhile, has maintained that Ukraine would be willing to halt attacks on Russian oil refineries if Moscow agreed to stop targeting Ukrainian power plants and other critical infrastructure.
The two countries have increasingly targeted each other's energy systems throughout the war, although the consequences have differed.

Russian strikes on Ukraine's power grid have left civilians facing electricity disruptions and damaged infrastructure needed to heat homes and sustain businesses. Ukrainian attacks on Russian refineries, meanwhile, have disrupted fuel production and exports, putting additional pressure on global energy markets.
The Trump administration has spent weeks attempting to negotiate a reciprocal halt to energy attacks as part of broader diplomatic efforts to bring an end to the war.
In September, Trump similarly announced that both countries had agreed to an energy ceasefire, although Moscow did not publicly confirm the agreement and attacks continued.

National security experts told Fox News Digital that Russia is facing tangible consequences for the war through its network of proxy countries that have directly endured the might of the U.S. military and subsequently left Russia with fewer streams of revenue and resources.  (Andrew Harnik/Getty Images)
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
The latest announcement raises the possibility of renewed diplomatic progress, but an energy ceasefire would not amount to a comprehensive agreement to end the fighting.

It was not immediately clear how the agreement would be monitored or enforced. The White House did not immediately respond to Fox News Digital's request for comment. Fox News Digital reached out to the Ukrainian and Russian embassies in Washington, D.C., seeking confirmation of the ceasefire but did not immediately receive responses.
Amanda Macias covers the intersection of business, economics and politics, with a focus on how policy decisions shape markets, businesses and American workers.

title: Minnesota GOP chair blasts progressive group over KKK-themed sign shown during Black House speaker's remarks
summary: Sunrise Movement Twin Cities said it disrupted a Minnesota Republican Party fundraiser, displaying a "RepubliKKKan Party" banner during Lisa Demuth's remarks.
story: Minnesota GOP gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth tells Fox News Digital that she understands Minnesotans' desire to end fraud and making living in the state affordable. She promises to deliver that if elected in November.

Minnesota's Republican Party chairman is accusing protesters of racial intimidation after demonstrators disrupted a GOP dinner and displayed a sign invoking the Ku Klux Klan while the state's first Black female House speaker addressed the crowd.

Minnesota GOP Chair Alex Plechash blasted the demonstrators in a statement after Friday night's Lincoln Reagan Dinner in Eagan, where protesters held a sign reading "RepubliKKKan Party" during remarks by House Speaker and Republican gubernatorial candidate Lisa Demuth.

"Last night, radical protesters stormed the stage at our Lincoln Reagan Dinner and held up a KKK symbol while Speaker Lisa Demuth spoke," Plechash said in a statement posted to X by the Republican Party of Minnesota.
DAVID MARCUS: MINNESOTA GOP CANDIDATES KEEP TRUMP AT ARM'S LENGTH AS THEY EYE A POST-TRUMP PARTY FUTURE
"Let's be clear about what happened. Left leaning protesters aimed a symbol of racial terror at a Black woman leader, at a dinner named for the president who ended slavery," he continued.

Sunrise Movement Twin Cities, a progressive activist organization, claimed responsibility for the disruption and said the demonstration was intended to protest Republican policies it believes harm immigrants and marginalized communities, according to local news station KTSP.

Gubernatorial nominee and state House Speaker Lisa Demuth speaks during the second day of the Minnesota Republican state convention at the Duluth Entertainment Convention Center (DECC) in Duluth, Minn., on Saturday, May 30, 2026. (Richard Tsong-Taatarii/The Minnesota Star Tribune via Getty Images)
"We disrupted this fundraiser because we refuse to give a moment's peace to the people bankrolling racial violence," the group said in a statement cited by the outlet.
The organization also said it was not affiliated with Minnesota's Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party (DFL).
Video of the incident shows demonstrators moving toward the front of the room holding signs, including one with the letters "KKK" highlighted in red, according to outlet.
One protester could be heard shouting, "You love Trump and you will not stand up for Minnesotans," as Demuth stood on stage holding a microphone.

Then-Minnesota House Minority Leader Lisa Demuth speaks at a rally for then-former President Donald Trump on July 27, 2024, at the Herb Brooks National Hockey Center in St. Cloud, Minnesota. (USA TODAY Network via Reuters Connect)
As security escorted the demonstrators away, attendees began chanting, "Lisa," followed by chants of, "USA."
Plechash told the outlet that protesters gained access to the dinner by purchasing tickets and passing through security checkpoints.
KLOBUCHAR'S FRAUD FIGHT CLAIM TAKES HIT AFTER GOP OPPONENT COMBS THROUGH RECEIPTS: 'WHERE WERE YOU?'
The chairman said the event experienced two disruptions, the first during remarks by Republican U.S. Senate candidate Michele Tafoya and the second while Demuth was speaking.

Plechash said roughly three or four protesters pushed toward the front of the room carrying banners during Demuth's remarks. He estimated the disruption lasted about 30 seconds and said he did not believe the demonstrators posed a physical threat.
Plechash said in his X post that Eagan police issued trespass orders and that potential charges remained under investigation.
The GOP chairman also called out Minnesota Democrats, specifically naming the Democratic-Farmer-Labor Party, Sen. Amy Klobuchar and Lt. Gov. Peggy Flanagan.

Sen. Amy Klobuchar (D-MN) speaks during a rally in support of a "Yes" vote on Proposition 50, a congressional redistricting measure in the November 4 special election, at the Los Angeles Convention Center in Los Angeles, California, on November 1, 2025. (David Swanson/REUTERS)
"Intimidation, criminal behavior, and racist rhetoric have no place in Minnesota politics," Plechash wrote.
"Republicans debate ideas, and we'd welcome the DFL to show up and do the same," he added. "Every hour they stay silent says something. Their silence is deafening."
CLICK HERE TO DOWNLOAD THE FOX NEWS APP
Demuth, who won Minnesota's Republican gubernatorial primary in August, will face off against Klobuchar, the Democratic nominee, in November's election to succeed Gov. Tim Walz.

title: NYC councilwoman blasts Mamdani over Italian Heritage Month post praising ‘communist’
summary: Vickie Paladino slammed Zohran Mamdani for honoring a congressman with Communist Party ties during Italian Heritage Month, calling it propaganda.
story: 'Fox & Friends Weekend' co-hosts discuss New York City Mayor Zohran Mamdani skipping a Columbus Day parade in Astoria after his past criticisms of Christopher Columbus. They also discuss his previous slights at Italian-Americans.

Mayor Zohran Mamdani’s Italian Heritage Month tribute to a left-wing congressman with ties to the Communist Party drew sharp criticism on social media, including a blistering rebuke from Queens Councilwoman Vickie Paladino.
"Happy Italian Heritage Month, New York. Here’s continuing to fight for Vito Marcantonio’s vision of a government that works for all working people," Mamdani wrote on X.

Marcantonio represented East Harlem in Congress for seven terms, first as a Republican and later as a member of the left-wing American Labor Party. His opposition to U.S. involvement in the Korean War and his legal work for the Communist Party drew FBI attention, the bureau kept files on him during the Cold War.
I ESCAPED COMMUNISM. AMERICA MUST NOT IGNORE THE URGENT WARNING SIGNS
Paladino called Marcantonio an "obscure Italian-American communist" and accused Mamdani of promoting communist propaganda.
"Of all the great men and women of Italian descent who've contributed to New York City and the United States, this is the idiot he picks," Paladino wrote on X.
MAMDANI DEFENDS CONTROVERSIAL NYC MAP AFTER OMITTING ICONIC LITTLE ITALY, JEWISH AND IRISH NEIGHBORHOODS
She urged Mamdani to stop invoking his Italian heritage, saying he was "physically incapable of being anything other than a loathsome propagandist for communism."

Paladino contrasted the mayor’s message with her family’s history. She said her father fought in World War II against Italian forces under Benito Mussolini, while her mother raised five children on her own and worked in a button factory.

"We wanted to become Americans, and our people were proud to learn the language and wave the American flag," she wrote. "That’s what being an Italian-American in New York means," Paladino added. "Not the communist propaganda Zohran is pushing here."
